one: Encryption hides data and can be reversed with a key. Hashing is one-way fingerprinting. Signing proves who produced data and that it was not changed.
an: Encryption is a locked box. A hash is a fingerprint. A signature is a wax seal with your personal crest.
how: Symmetric encryption (AES): one shared key, fast. Asymmetric (RSA, elliptic curve): public key encrypts or verifies, private key decrypts or signs.
In transit (TLS) vs at rest (disk/DB encryption, usually managed by the cloud with a KMS). Field-level encryption for especially sensitive columns.
HMAC: a hash keyed with a secret, used to sign webhooks and cookies. Compare signatures with a constant-time function.
why: Picking the wrong primitive is a classic mistake: encrypting passwords (should hash), hashing tokens you need to read back (should encrypt), trusting unsigned data.
trade: Never invent crypto. Use well-known libraries and managed key services; the hard part is key management, not the algorithm.

myth.r: Base64 is encoding. Anyone can decode it instantly.

q.s: Your server must store users' third-party API tokens and use them later to call that API. Right primitive?
o: Hash them with bcrypt
Encrypt them (ideally with a KMS-managed key)
Base64 them
Store plain text
q.e: You need the original value back, so hashing is out. Encryption with managed keys is the answer.

more: Authenticated encryption (AES-GCM) and why plain encryption is not enough
lab: Use Node's crypto to encrypt and decrypt a string with AES-256-GCM; tamper with the ciphertext and see decryption fail.
Generate an Ed25519 key pair, sign a message, verify it, then change one byte and verify again.

plain: Three different tools, often confused. Encryption hides data; with the key you can get the original back. Hashing makes a one-way fingerprint; you can never get the original back. Signing proves who created data and that nobody changed it.
bridge: HTTPS uses encryption. Password storage uses hashing. JWTs and webhooks use signatures. Base64 (which you see everywhere) is none of these; it is just encoding anyone can reverse.

walk.title: Choosing the right tool for three jobs
steps: Storing user passwords: you never need the original back, only to compare. → Hash (Argon2id).
Storing users' connected Google tokens: you need the original to call Google later. → Encrypt (with a key in a key management service).
Sending “order 42 paid” to a partner: they must know it came from you and was not changed. → Sign (HMAC or a private key).
Sending anything over the network: → TLS/HTTPS (encryption in transit).
Using the wrong tool (e.g. encrypting passwords) creates a hidden weakness.

terms: Reversible hiding of data with a key.
One shared key / a public and private key pair.
Key management service: stores and uses keys for you.
insights: Before encrypting a field, ask where the key lives. If the app server holds both the data and the key, encryption at rest only protects stolen disks and backups.
Encryption at rest is usually a checkbox in managed services; turn it on.
Store a key version with every ciphertext from day one; adding it later means migrating every row.

prod.summary: In production, the algorithm choice is easy (AES-256-GCM, TLS 1.2+/1.3, Ed25519 or ECDSA); the hard and failure-prone parts are keys and nonces: where keys live, who can use them, how they rotate, and making sure the same nonce is never reused with the same key. Seniors check that keys are in a KMS or secret manager, that encryption is authenticated, and that every ciphertext records which key version made it.
checklist: Use authenticated encryption (AES-256-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305), never AES-CBC or ECB without a MAC.
Each GCM encryption uses a fresh random 96-bit IV; IV, auth tag and key version are stored next to the ciphertext.
Data keys are wrapped by a KMS key (envelope encryption); the master key never leaves the KMS.
Key rotation is possible without downtime: new writes use the new key, old ciphertext is decrypted by key version and re-encrypted in the background.
Bind ciphertext to its context with associated data (e.g. the row ID and column name), so a value cannot be copied to another row.
TLS 1.2 is the minimum on public endpoints; TLS 1.0/1.1 are disabled.
Searchable sensitive fields (email lookups) use a separate keyed hash (HMAC) column, not deterministic encryption built by hand.
numbers: AES-GCM standard IV size is 96 bits (12 bytes); the auth tag is 128 bits (16 bytes).
NIST SP 800-38D: with random 96-bit IVs, limit one key to about 2^32 (4.3 billion) encryptions to keep IV collision risk acceptable.
AWS KMS Encrypt accepts at most 4,096 bytes of plaintext, which is why large data uses envelope encryption with GenerateDataKey.
AWS KMS automatic key rotation for customer-managed keys is yearly by default (configurable from 90 to 2,560 days).
failures: Decryption fails with Unsupported state or unable to authenticate data after a deploy.

Wrong key version, wrong IV, or a missing or truncated auth tag (often the column was too short, or base64 vs hex mismatch). Store key version + IV + tag + ciphertext together in one versioned format.
Security review: the same IV is used for every encryption (“IV = 0, it is just a constant”).
With GCM, nonce reuse under one key leaks the XOR of plaintexts and lets attackers forge messages. Use crypto.randomBytes(12) per encryption and rotate the key used so far.
The encryption key is in .env next to the database URL; a leaked backup and the env file are both stolen.
Encryption then protected nothing. Keep keys in a KMS or secret manager with separate access, and use envelope encryption so a DB dump alone is useless.
Customers' encrypted API tokens can be swapped between rows by someone with DB write access.
Ciphertext is not bound to its row. Pass the row ID as AAD (associated data) when encrypting and decrypting.

code.title: AES-256-GCM field encryption with key versions and AAD
code.note: The key version prefix makes rotation possible, and the AAD ties the value to one row and column, so it cannot be moved.

qs.s: A service encrypts tokens with AES-256-CBC and a random IV, but no MAC. An attacker can change ciphertext in the database and watch whether the app returns “decrypt error” or “invalid token”. What is the risk, and the fix?
o: None, AES-256 is unbreakable
Use a longer key
Base64-encode the result
Padding-oracle attacks can recover plaintext; use authenticated encryption (AES-GCM) so any change fails before decryption is used
qs.e: Unauthenticated CBC plus different error messages is a classic padding oracle. Authenticated encryption detects tampering. A longer key does not help at all.

qs.s: You must encrypt 50 MB files with AWS KMS. Calling KMS Encrypt fails. Why, and what is the standard pattern?
o: KMS Encrypt takes at most 4 KB; use envelope encryption: get a data key from GenerateDataKey, encrypt the file locally with it, store the wrapped data key next to the file
KMS is too slow; store the master key in the app instead
Split the file into 4 KB parts and call KMS for each
Use S3 without encryption
qs.e: Envelope encryption keeps the master key in KMS and does bulk work locally. Calling KMS for every 4 KB chunk works technically but is slow, expensive and hits KMS rate limits.

qs.s: You need to find users by email, but emails must be encrypted at rest. A teammate suggests AES with a fixed IV so the same email always gives the same ciphertext. Better approach?
o: The fixed IV is fine for emails
Hash the email with plain SHA-256 and search by that
Encrypt with random IVs, and add a separate HMAC-SHA256(key, normalized email) column for lookups
Do not encrypt emails
qs.e: A fixed IV with GCM breaks its security. Plain SHA-256 of an email can be reversed by guessing common emails. A keyed HMAC gives a stable lookup value that is useless without the key.

qs.s: This code runs in 8 pods that share one key from the secret manager. What is the bug?

code.title: crypto.ts

o: The IV should be 16 bytes for AES-256
The auth tag is stored before the ciphertext
A counter IV is predictable, which breaks GCM

Every pod (and every restart) starts at 0, so the same key and IV pair is used many times. GCM nonce reuse leaks plaintext relationships and lets attackers forge messages. Use crypto.randomBytes(12) per message
qs.e: GCM needs IVs that are unique per key, not secret or unpredictable, so a counter is fine only if it is never reset and never shared. Across pods and restarts that is hard; random 96-bit IVs are the simple choice (up to about 2^32 messages per key). The 12-byte IV is the standard size.

qs.s: Customers get API keys (32 random bytes) for your public API. How should the server store them?
o: Store a SHA-256 (or HMAC) of the key with a short visible prefix for lookup and display; show the full key only once at creation
Encrypt them with AES so you can show them again later
Hash them with Argon2id, like passwords
Store them in plain text in a separate table
qs.e: You never need the key back, only to check it, so hash it. Because the key is high-entropy random data, a fast hash is enough and allows an indexed lookup. A prefix (like sk_live_ab12…) helps users identify keys and helps secret scanners find leaked ones.

qs.s: A security scan flags this nginx config. What is the finding?

code.title: nginx.conf

o: The certificate path is wrong
TLS 1.0 and 1.1 are enabled; they were formally deprecated in 2021 (RFC 8996). Use ssl_protocols TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3;
TLS 1.3 should be disabled because it is too new
HIGH ciphers are too slow
qs.e: Modern browsers already refuse TLS 1.0/1.1, so leaving them on only helps downgrade attempts and old, unpatched clients. Check real client support first (for example old embedded devices), then remove them.

qs.s: You enable automatic yearly rotation on the AWS KMS key that wraps your data keys. Do you need to re-encrypt existing data?
o: Yes, immediately; old ciphertext can no longer be decrypted
Yes, because rotation deletes the old key material
No: KMS keeps all old key material and picks the right version on decrypt. But rotation does not help if a data key or plaintext already leaked; that needs re-encryption with new data keys
No, and rotation also re-encrypts all your S3 objects
qs.e: KMS rotation only changes which key material encrypts new data. It is cheap hygiene, not incident response. If you suspect a leak of a data key, generate new data keys and re-encrypt the affected data.

interview.q: Explain envelope encryption and why systems use it.
answer: A KMS holds a key-encryption key (KEK) that never leaves it. For each object or record set, the app asks for a data key (DEK): it gets the plaintext DEK and a copy wrapped by the KEK.
The app encrypts data locally with the DEK (AES-256-GCM), stores the wrapped DEK next to the ciphertext, and throws away the plaintext DEK.
To decrypt, the app sends only the small wrapped DEK to KMS; bulk data never travels to KMS.
Benefits: no size limits (KMS Encrypt takes 4 KB), fewer KMS calls, access controlled and logged by KMS IAM policies.
Trade-off: caching DEKs saves cost and latency but widens exposure; set cache lifetimes and limits.
followups: How would you rotate the KEK?
How do you make a backup useless to someone who steals it?

interview.q: We must encrypt national ID numbers in a column but still find users by ID number. Design it.
answer: Encrypt the value with AES-256-GCM, random IV, key from KMS, AAD bound to the row and column.
Add a separate blind index: HMAC-SHA256(indexKey, normalize(value)) in its own column with a unique index; search by computing the same HMAC.
Use a different key for the index than for encryption, and normalise carefully (spaces, dashes).
Risk: equal values have equal HMACs, so frequency is visible; truncating the HMAC adds false positives and reduces that leak.
Restrict who can decrypt: most code paths only need the index, not the plaintext.
followups: Why not deterministic encryption?
How would you support “starts with” search?

interview.q: When do you use symmetric encryption, asymmetric crypto, or HMAC? Give examples from a web app.
answer: Symmetric (AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305): fast bulk encryption when the same party encrypts and decrypts, e.g. encrypting stored OAuth tokens.
Asymmetric signatures (Ed25519, ECDSA, RSA): many parties verify, one signs; e.g. JWTs checked by many services, package signing.
Asymmetric key exchange: inside TLS to agree on symmetric session keys; you rarely use it directly.
HMAC: both sides share a secret and need integrity, e.g. webhook signatures, signed cookies, signed URLs.
Hashes without keys: integrity of public data (checksums), never for secrets with low entropy.
followups: Why is AES-CBC without a MAC a problem?
When would you pick Ed25519 over HMAC for webhooks?

diagrams.title: Pick the tool by the job
diagrams.src:
flowchart TD
  J{"What does the data need?"}
  J -- "compare only, e.g. passwords" --> H["Hash: Argon2id"]
  J -- "read back later, e.g. Google tokens" --> E["Encrypt: AES-256-GCM, key in a KMS"]
  J -- "prove sender, nothing changed" --> S["Sign: HMAC or private key"]
  J -- "safe on the network" --> T["TLS / HTTPS"]
  B["Base64"] --> N["Not protection: anyone decodes it"]
diagrams.caption: What to notice: the question is never “which is most secure?” but “what must happen to this data later?”. Base64 is only encoding and answers none of these jobs.

diagrams.title: Envelope encryption with a KMS
diagrams.src:
sequenceDiagram
  participant App
  participant KMS
  participant DB
  App->>KMS: GenerateDataKey for master key
  KMS-->>App: data key in plain + same key encrypted
  App->>App: AES-256-GCM with data key, fresh 12-byte IV
  App->>DB: ciphertext, IV, tag, encrypted data key
  Note over KMS: the master key never leaves the KMS
  Note over App,DB: to read: KMS decrypts the data key, the app decrypts locally
diagrams.caption: What to notice: a database dump alone is useless, because the data key stored next to the data is itself encrypted by a key the attacker cannot export.

codeCheck.detail: Round trip works; a wrong AAD and a flipped ciphertext byte both throw on the auth tag; a value written under key v1 still decrypts after CURRENT moved to v2.

videos.t: 7 Cryptography Concepts EVERY Developer Should Know
videos.why: Hash, salt, HMAC, symmetric, asymmetric and signing with code.

videos.t: What are Digital Signatures? - Computerphile
videos.why: What a digital signature proves.

one: A signature made with a shared secret that proves a message came from someone who knows the secret and was not modified.
an: A secret handshake that also depends on what you are saying: change one word and the handshake no longer matches.
how: signature = HMAC_SHA256(secret, rawBody). The receiver recomputes and compares.
Verify against the raw bytes of the body, before JSON parsing reformats it. Compare with a constant-time function to avoid timing attacks.
Include a timestamp in what is signed and reject old messages to prevent replays.
why: Webhooks, signed cookies, presigned URLs and payment callbacks all rely on it.
trade: Shared secrets must be stored and rotated like passwords. Asymmetric signatures avoid sharing a secret, at more complexity.

myth.m: Checking the sender's IP is enough to trust a webhook.
myth.r: IPs change and can be spoofed in some setups. Signatures are the reliable check.

q.s: Webhook signature checks keep failing even though the secret is correct. Common cause?
o: Wrong DNS
Verifying a re-serialised JSON body instead of the exact raw request bytes
TLS
CORS
q.e: Whitespace or key order changes break the signature. Capture the raw body for verification.

more: Key rotation with multiple valid secrets
lab: Write a webhook receiver that verifies HMAC_SHA256(secret, timestamp + '.' + rawBody) and rejects messages older than 5 minutes.
Write a signed-URL helper for downloads that expires after 60 seconds.

plain: HMAC is a signature made with a shared secret. The sender computes a code from the message and the secret; the receiver does the same calculation and compares. If anyone changed even one character, or does not know the secret, the codes will not match.
bridge: Stripe (Stripe-Signature), GitHub (X-Hub-Signature-256) and Shopify (X-Shopify-Hmac-Sha256) sign their webhooks with HMAC-SHA256, and the verification snippet in their docs is exactly this. (Telegram bot webhooks are different: they only send a static secret header, X-Telegram-Bot-Api-Secret-Token; Telegram Mini App initData is HMAC-signed.)

walk.title: Verifying a webhook
steps: The provider computes HMAC_SHA256(secret, timestamp + '.' + rawBody) and sends it in a header along with the timestamp.
Your server reads the raw body bytes (before parsing JSON) and the timestamp.
It computes the same HMAC with its copy of the secret.
It compares with a constant-time function and checks the timestamp is recent (e.g. under 5 minutes).
Match and fresh: process. Otherwise: reject. Someone who changed the amount, or replays an old message, fails.

terms: Hash-based message authentication code: a keyed signature.
Comparison that takes the same time whether it fails early or late.
insights: A valid signature proves who sent a message, not that you are seeing it for the first time. Deduplicate by event ID.
Signed download URLs use the same idea: the link carries an expiry and a signature.
When a provider offers public-key signatures, you verify with a public key and have no shared secret to protect or rotate on your side.

prod.summary: In production, HMAC verification fails in boring ways: a body parser changed the bytes, the secret has a trailing newline, the comparison is not constant-time, or nobody checks the timestamp so old events can be replayed. Seniors check raw-body handling, replay windows, idempotency on the event ID, and that secret rotation accepts two secrets during the overlap.
checklist: The signature is computed over the raw request bytes, captured before any JSON parsing.
Comparison uses crypto.timingSafeEqual on equal-length buffers.
A timestamp is part of the signed data and events older than about 5 minutes are rejected.
Event IDs are stored, and duplicates are ignored (providers retry, and replay inside the window is still possible).
Secret rotation: the receiver accepts the old and the new secret for a period, then removes the old one.
Secrets are per integration or per customer, not one global secret for all webhook senders.
Verification failures are counted and alerted; a sudden jump means a broken deploy or an attack.
numbers: Stripe's official libraries reject webhook events with a timestamp older than 300 seconds (5 minutes) by default.
GitHub signs with HMAC-SHA256 in X-Hub-Signature-256: sha256=… and does not sign a timestamp, so replay protection must use the X-GitHub-Delivery ID.
Standard Webhooks signs msg_id.timestamp.body and sends webhook-id, webhook-timestamp and webhook-signature headers.
HMAC-SHA256 output is 32 bytes (64 hex characters).
failures: Every webhook fails with “No signatures found matching the expected signature for payload”.

The framework parsed the JSON before verification (e.g. global express.json()), so the bytes changed. Mount express.raw({ type: 'application/json' }) on the webhook route, or read await req.text() in a Next.js route handler.
Signatures fail only in production; locally they pass.
The production secret was pasted with a trailing newline or space, or staging and production secrets are swapped. Trim on load and log a hash prefix of the secret (never the secret) to compare.
The same “payment succeeded” event is processed twice, creating two orders.
Providers retry on timeouts, and signatures stay valid. Store the event ID with a unique constraint and skip duplicates; respond 2xx quickly and process in a queue.
Pentest: signature check is bypassed by sending the header sha256= with an empty value.

The code used expected.startsWith(given), or caught the error timingSafeEqual throws on a length mismatch and treated it as success. Reject missing or wrong-length signatures explicitly, then compare.

code.title: Verify a signed webhook with a replay window
code.note: !(age <= TOLERANCE_S) also rejects NaN from a missing or non-numeric timestamp. Two secrets are accepted so rotation causes no failures.

qs.s: An attacker captures a valid signed webhook (“refund order 42”) and re-sends it an hour later. The receiver verifies HMAC over the body only. What stops the replay?
o: TLS prevents capture, so it cannot happen
HMAC includes the time automatically
Nothing; the signature is still valid. Sign a timestamp too, reject old messages, and store processed event IDs
Constant-time comparison
qs.e: HMAC proves origin and integrity, not freshness. Freshness needs a signed timestamp and/or a stored nonce/event ID.

qs.s: Code: if (expectedHex === req.get('X-Signature')) …. What is the theoretical problem, and the fix?
o: Hex is not secure, use base64
String === can stop at the first different character, leaking timing; compare buffers with crypto.timingSafeEqual after checking lengths
It should use ==
Headers are case-sensitive
qs.e: A timing leak lets an attacker guess the signature byte by byte in theory. Over a network it is hard, but the fix is cheap and standard.

qs.s: You need to rotate a webhook secret shared with a partner without dropping events. Which plan works?
o: Change it on both sides at the same second
Disable verification during the change
Use the new secret only for GET requests
Accept both old and new secrets on the receiver, switch the sender to the new one, then remove the old one after traffic confirms it
qs.e: An overlap window avoids a coordinated cut-over. Disabling verification, even briefly, opens the endpoint to forged events.

qs.s: Read this Next.js route handler for a webhook. Signatures fail for most real events. What is the correct fix?

code.title: app/api/webhooks/route.ts

o: Use digest('base64') instead of hex
Read await req.text(), compute the HMAC over that exact string, compare with crypto.timingSafeEqual after a length check, and only then JSON.parse it
Sort the JSON keys before signing
Trim whitespace from the secret and keep the rest
qs.e: JSON.stringify(JSON.parse(x)) is not byte-identical to x (spacing, key order, unicode escapes), so the HMAC differs. Sorting keys still changes bytes. The !== comparison is a second, smaller problem; fix both.

qs.s: Read this signed-download helper. Which problem does it have?

code.title: signed-url.ts

o: base64url is not safe in URLs
HMAC-SHA256 is too short for URLs
The expiry should be in milliseconds

Ambiguous input: '12' + '1924992000' and '1' + '21924992000' are the same string, so a link for file 12 can be turned into a link for file 1 that expires centuries later. Sign an unambiguous encoding (fixed field separator that cannot appear in values, or JSON) and include the purpose
qs.e: HMAC protects bytes, not meaning. When fields are concatenated without a separator, different field values produce the same bytes. Use something like `download:${fileId}:${expiresAt}` with IDs that cannot contain :, and reject expiry values far in the future.

qs.s: Your platform sends webhooks to 5,000 customer endpoints. Which signing design is right?
o: A separate secret per customer endpoint (or asymmetric signatures with your public key published), so one customer cannot forge events to another
One global HMAC secret, given to all customers, rotated yearly
No signature; HTTPS is enough
Sign with the customer's API key
qs.e: With one shared secret, every customer knows the key that signs everyone's events and can forge events to any other customer. Per-endpoint secrets limit a leak to one customer. Asymmetric signatures (Standard Webhooks supports Ed25519) avoid shared secrets completely, at the cost of a little more complexity for receivers.

qs.s: A legacy service signs messages like this. Why does a reviewer ask to replace it with HMAC?

code.title: legacy-sign.ts

o: SHA-256 is broken
Hashes are slower than HMAC
SHA-256 and similar hashes allow length extension: knowing H(secret || m), an attacker can compute a valid signature for m plus extra data without the secret. HMAC's construction prevents this
Only because HMAC output is shorter
qs.e: SHA-256 itself is fine; the construction is not. HMAC hashes the key and message in two nested passes, which blocks length extension and is the standard way to build a MAC from a hash.

interview.q: Design webhook delivery for our platform: signing, retries, replay protection and secret rotation.
answer: Sign id.timestamp.body with HMAC-SHA256 per endpoint secret (the Standard Webhooks format), sending webhook-id, webhook-timestamp and webhook-signature.
Receivers verify over raw bytes, reject timestamps outside about 5 minutes, and dedupe by event ID.
Retries with exponential backoff over hours or days, at-least-once delivery, so idempotency on the receiver is required; disable endpoints that fail for too long and notify the owner.
Rotation: allow two active secrets per endpoint, sign with both (several signatures in the header) during the overlap.
Send from isolated workers through an SSRF-safe client, with timeouts and no internal network access.
followups: How would receivers verify ordering?
When would you choose Ed25519 instead of HMAC?

interview.q: Why HMAC instead of hash(secret + message)? And why constant-time comparison?
answer: Plain secret-prefix hashing with SHA-256/SHA-1 is open to length-extension attacks; HMAC's nested construction is not, and it is proven secure if the hash is a good PRF.
HMAC is standard and available everywhere (crypto.createHmac), so there is no reason to build your own.
Normal string comparison can return early at the first different byte; in theory an attacker can measure timing and guess a signature byte by byte.
crypto.timingSafeEqual needs equal-length buffers, so check length first and treat a mismatch as failure, not as an exception to ignore.
Over a network the timing attack is hard, but the fix is free.
followups: Is SHA-3 vulnerable to length extension?
Why compare raw bytes instead of hex strings?

interview.q: Webhook signature errors jumped right after a deploy. How do you debug it?
answer: Look at what changed: body parsing middleware, framework upgrade, proxy, secret configuration.
Check raw-body handling: a global JSON parser or a new compression or proxy layer that changes the bytes.
Check the secret: newline or whitespace, wrong environment, base64 vs raw secret (some providers' secrets are base64 with a prefix such as whsec_). Log a short hash of the secret, never the secret.
Check time: clock drift on new hosts makes timestamps look old; ensure NTP.
Replay one failing request locally with the stored headers and body to reproduce, then add a test with a real recorded payload.
followups: What metrics would have caught this sooner?
Would you ever turn verification off temporarily?

sequenceDiagram
  participant P as Provider
  participant X as Attacker
  participant S as Your server
  P->>P: sig = HMAC_SHA256(secret, timestamp + '.' + rawBody)
  P->>S: POST event + timestamp + signature headers

  S-->>P: 200, duplicate event ID skipped
diagrams.caption: What to notice: the signature stops changes, the timestamp stops old replays, and the stored event ID stops duplicates inside the 5-minute window. You need all three.

codeCheck.detail: Valid signature -> 200; tampered body, 301 s-old or NaN timestamp, and unknown secret -> 400; the old secret is accepted during rotation and events are deduped by id.

one: Give every user, service and key only the access it needs, and layer several independent defences so one failure is not fatal.
an: A castle with a moat, walls, an inner keep and guards, where each guard only has keys to their own tower.
how: In PostgreSQL, only the table owner (or a superuser) can DROP or ALTER a table, so the app should connect as a role that owns nothing and has only SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE grants; migrations run as a separate owner role. Read-only credentials for analytics; per-service API keys with narrow scopes; admin access through short-lived elevation.
Layers: network isolation, authentication, authorization checks, input validation, encryption, monitoring and alerting, backups.
Plan for blast radius: if this key leaks, what can the attacker do?
why: Breaches are rarely one bug. They are one bug plus excessive access. Limiting access turns breaches into contained incidents.
trade: Every restriction adds friction. Automate access requests and use roles so security does not become a bottleneck.

myth.m: Our network is private, so internal services can trust each other.
myth.r: Zero-trust assumes an attacker may already be inside and verifies each call.

q.s: A reporting tool needs to read sales tables. What credentials should it get?
o: The app's main DB user
A read-only role limited to the reporting tables or a replica
The superuser
Shared admin password
q.e: If the reporting tool is compromised, it can read sales data but not change or delete anything.

more: Separate DB roles for app, migrations and analytics
lab: In Postgres, create roles: app_rw (no DDL), migrator (DDL), analytics_ro (SELECT only). Point each tool at its role.
For one of your projects, list every credential and what an attacker could do with each. Shrink the worst one.

plain:
Least privilege: every person, program and key gets only the access it truly needs. Defence in depth: several independent layers of protection, so one failure is not a disaster.

The question to ask about anything: if this leaked, what could an attacker do?
bridge: It is the same thinking as giving a component only the props it needs instead of the whole app state: smaller surface, smaller damage when something goes wrong.

walk.title: Shrinking the damage of a leaked key
steps: Your reporting tool connects to the database with the same user as the app: full read and write, including DROP TABLE.
Its credentials leak through a misconfigured dashboard.
With those rights, the attacker could read, change or delete everything.
Better: a separate read-only role that can only SELECT from reporting views, ideally on a replica.
Same leak now: the attacker can read some sales numbers. Bad, but contained and recoverable.

terms: Minimum access needed for the job.
How much damage one compromised thing can cause.
Verify every request, even inside your own network.
insights: Short-lived credentials (IAM roles, OIDC from CI) limit a leak in time; narrow permissions limit it in scope. You want both.
Separate credentials per tool and per environment, so one leak does not expose everything.
Make the safe path easy (roles, templates), or people will share admin keys to save time.

prod.summary: In production, least privilege is less about one perfect policy and more about inventory: every key, role and token, who uses it, and what it can do. Seniors look for shared admin credentials, wildcards in IAM policies, long-lived keys where short-lived ones are possible, and CI tokens with write access to everything. The goal is that any one leak becomes a contained incident.
checklist: Separate DB roles: app (DML only, owns nothing), migrator (owner, used only in deploys), analytics (read-only, ideally on a replica).
No IAM policies with "Action": "*" or "Resource": "*" for workloads; use access analysis tools to trim unused permissions.
Workloads use short-lived credentials (IAM roles, workload identity, OIDC from CI) instead of static access keys.
GitHub Actions workflows set permissions: explicitly (start with contents: read).
Production access for humans is time-limited and logged (just-in-time elevation, break-glass account with alerts).
Services talk to each other with authentication (mTLS or signed tokens), even inside the VPC.
Each credential has an owner and a rotation date; unused ones are removed.
numbers: Since PostgreSQL 15, the PUBLIC role no longer has CREATE on the public schema by default.
AWS IAM role sessions last 1 hour by default (configurable up to 12 hours).
GitHub's default GITHUB_TOKEN permission for new repositories and organizations is read-only for repository contents.
failures: A SQL injection in a search endpoint led to DROP TABLE orders.
The app connected as the table owner. Move ownership to a migrator role, grant the app only DML, and make deploys use the migrator credentials.
A leaked CI token pushed malicious code to the main branch and published a package.
The token had write access to everything. Use OIDC/trusted publishing for releases, scope workflow permissions per job, and protect branches so tokens cannot bypass review.
Contractor's laptop stolen; it had a long-lived AWS access key with AdministratorAccess.
Static keys with admin rights. Revoke the key, review CloudTrail for its use, move humans to SSO with short sessions and role-specific permissions.
An internal metrics service was used to read customer data after an attacker got into one pod.
Flat network and no service authentication. Add network policies (default deny), and require service identity on internal APIs.

code.title: Separate PostgreSQL roles for owner, app and analytics
code.note: ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES is the line teams forget: without it, the next migration creates a table the app cannot read, and someone “fixes” it by making the app the owner.

qs.s: After a migration adds a new table, the app fails with permission denied for table invoices. A teammate wants to make the app role the owner of all tables to stop this happening. Better fix?
o: Make the app role a superuser
Grant ALL PRIVILEGES on the database
Add ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES FOR ROLE migrator … GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON TABLES TO app_rw
Run the app as the migrator role
qs.e: Default privileges give new tables the right grants automatically. Making the app the owner gives it DROP and ALTER, which is exactly the access least privilege removes.

qs.s: A GitHub Actions workflow only runs tests on pull requests, but has no permissions: block in an old organization where the default token is read/write. What is the risk?
o: A compromised test dependency or action could use the write token to push code or change releases
Tests run slower
None, tokens expire after the job
Pull requests cannot run
qs.e: The token is short-lived, but during the job it can do anything its permissions allow. Set permissions: contents: read at the top and grant more per job only when needed.

qs.s: Which change reduces blast radius the most for a leaked credential?
o: Making the password longer
Rotating the credential every 90 days
Hiding it in an obfuscated config file
Replacing a long-lived admin key with short-lived, role-scoped credentials issued per workload
qs.e: Scope and lifetime decide what an attacker can do and for how long. Rotation every 90 days still leaves up to 90 days of full access.

qs.s: The upload service only writes and reads user avatars in this bucket. Review its IAM policy. What is the real problem?

code.title: avatar-service-policy.json

o: It can delete the whole bucket
Nothing; the resource is limited to one bucket
The service can delete or overwrite every object, change object ACLs and tags, not just read and write. Grant only s3:PutObject and s3:GetObject, ideally on a key prefix
It needs s3:ListAllMyBuckets to work
qs.e: The /* resource covers object-level actions only, so bucket actions like DeleteBucket do not match; that tempting answer is wrong. But s3:* on objects still means a compromised service can wipe every avatar or rewrite them. List only the actions the code calls.

qs.s: This workflow lints on pull requests and deploys from main. How should the permissions be set?

code.title: .github/workflows/ci.yml
code.src:
on: [push, pull_request]
permissions: write-all
jobs:
  lint:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: npm ci && npm run lint
  deploy:
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: ./deploy.sh   # uses OIDC to assume an AWS role

o: Top level permissions: contents: read; add id-token: write only on the deploy job, and limit the AWS role's trust policy to this repo's main branch
Keep write-all; the token expires after the job
Remove permissions entirely; the default is always read-only
Give id-token: write to all jobs so OIDC works everywhere
qs.e: Per-job permissions mean a compromised lint dependency cannot push code or mint cloud credentials. Defaults depend on organisation settings and repo age, so set them explicitly. The cloud side matters too: the role's trust policy should check the sub claim (repo and branch).

qs.s: A teammate runs GRANT ALL ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA app TO app_rw; to “fix permissions”. The tables are owned by migrator. Which statement is true?
o: app_rw can now DROP tables
app_rw still cannot drop or alter tables (that needs ownership), but it gained TRUNCATE, REFERENCES and TRIGGER (and MAINTAIN on PostgreSQL 17+), so one injection can empty a table instantly
Nothing changed; ALL means only SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE
app_rw becomes the owner of the tables
qs.e: Table privileges never include DROP; only the owner (or a member of the owning role, or a superuser) can drop. But ALL includes privileges the app does not need. Grant the four DML privileges explicitly.

qs.s: A web pod in Kubernetes gets remote code execution through a library bug. The pod uses the namespace's default service account, and its token is mounted. What should have limited the damage?
o: Nothing; RCE in a pod means the cluster is lost
A larger memory limit
Running as root, so the logs show more

automountServiceAccountToken: false for pods that do not call the Kubernetes API, a dedicated service account with no RBAC bindings when they do not need any, non-root containers, and a default-deny NetworkPolicy
qs.e: A mounted token lets the attacker talk to the API server with whatever RBAC the account has, and default accounts often collect bindings over time. Each layer here removes one path: API access, privilege escalation in the container, lateral movement in the network.

interview.q: How do you apply least privilege to a typical web app's database, cloud and CI access?
answer: Database: app role with DML only on its schema, migrator role that owns objects, read-only analytics role on a replica, separate credentials per service.
Cloud: workload identities (IAM roles, workload identity federation) instead of static keys; policies with explicit actions and resources; access analysis to remove unused permissions.
CI: explicit workflow permissions, OIDC to the cloud with trust policies limited to repo and branch, secrets only in the jobs that need them, protected environments for production.
Humans: SSO, short sessions, just-in-time elevation for production, break-glass with alerts.
Keep an inventory: every credential has an owner, a scope and an expiry, and the blast radius of each is written down.
followups: How do you stop permissions from growing back over time?
What is the first thing you would fix in a startup with one shared admin key?

interview.q: Engineers need production access to debug incidents. How do you design it?
answer: Default: no standing access. Request elevation for a time window (e.g. 1–4 hours) with a ticket or incident link, approved or auto-approved during incidents.
Prefer read-only paths first: logs, traces, metrics, read replicas, masked data.
Sessions go through a bastion or session manager that records commands; no SSH keys on laptops.
Break-glass account for when SSO is down: stored offline, alerts on use, reviewed after.
Review access logs regularly, and make the safe path fast so people do not build workarounds.
followups: How do you handle customer data during debugging?
What would you alert on?

interview.q: Explain defence in depth with a concrete example where one layer failed and another held.
answer: Example: an SSRF bug in a URL fetcher (layer 1, input validation, failed).
Layer 2: the fetcher ran in a network segment with no route to internal services or the metadata endpoint, so internal targets were unreachable.
Layer 3: IMDSv2 and a minimal instance role meant even a metadata response would have had little value.
Layer 4: egress logs and alerts on blocked destinations showed the attempts within minutes.
Point: layers should be independent; two checks in the same code path fail together.
followups: How do you decide which layers are worth their cost?
What is zero trust in practice?

diagrams.title: Same leak, two setups
diagrams.src:
flowchart TD
  L["Reporting tool credentials leak"] --> Q{"Which database role?"}
  Q -- "same role as the app, owns tables" --> A["Read every table"]
  A --> A2["Change or delete any data"]
  A2 --> A3["DROP TABLE orders"]
  Q -- "analytics_ro, SELECT only" --> B["Read some sales numbers"]
  B --> B2["Cannot write, cannot DROP"]
  B2 --> B3["Contained, recoverable incident"]
diagrams.caption: What to notice: the leak is identical; only the permissions behind it differ. That difference is the blast radius.

codeCheck.detail: All three roles created with LOGIN; after a migrator-created table, ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES gave app_rw CRUD automatically; analytics_ro got statement_timeout=60s.

one: Ways to model permissions: by role, by attributes and rules, and enforced inside the database per row.
an: RBAC: job titles grant keys. ABAC: the door checks your department, the time and whether you own the room. RLS: the filing cabinet itself refuses to show folders that are not yours.
how: RBAC: users get roles, roles get permissions. Simple; explodes into dozens of roles when rules get specific.

ABAC / policies: allow edit if doc.ownerId == user.id or user.role == 'admin' and doc.orgId == user.orgId. Tools: OPA, Cerbos, Oso, CASL. ReBAC (relationship-based, Google Zanzibar style): OpenFGA, SpiceDB.

Row-Level Security (Postgres RLS, used heavily by Supabase): policies attached to tables filter rows by the current user automatically, even if app code forgets. Watch the exceptions: superusers, roles with BYPASSRLS (like Supabase's service_role/secret key) and, unless you use FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY, the table owner all skip the policies.
Multi-tenancy: every query must be scoped by tenant/org ID. RLS or a mandatory query layer prevents cross-tenant leaks.
why: Cross-tenant data leaks are among the worst incidents a SaaS can have. A systematic model beats scattered if-statements.
trade: RLS moves logic into the database, which some teams find harder to test and debug. Policies must be indexed-friendly or queries slow down.

myth.m: The Supabase public key in the frontend means the database is open.
myth.r: The anon key (or the newer sb_publishable_… key) is meant to be public. RLS policies are what protect the data, so tables without RLS enabled are the real hole. The secret/service_role key bypasses RLS and must never reach the browser.

q.s: A Supabase table has RLS disabled, and the client uses the public anon key. Impact?
o: None, the key is secret
Anyone can read (and possibly write) the whole table via the public API
Only admins can read
Queries are slower
q.e: Enable RLS on every exposed table and write explicit policies.

more: RLS performance and indexing policy columns
Tenant isolation strategies (shared table, schema per tenant, DB per tenant)
lab: Enable RLS on a Postgres table with an owner_id column and a policy using current_setting('app.user_id'). Prove one user cannot see another's rows even with SELECT *.
In Supabase, enable RLS on a table and write select/insert policies with auth.uid(); test with two accounts.

plain: Ways to organise permissions. RBAC: users have roles (admin, editor, viewer) and roles have permissions. ABAC: rules based on attributes (“owner of the document” or “same company”). Row-level security: the database itself filters rows per user, so even a forgotten check in code cannot leak data.
bridge: In Supabase, your frontend talks to the database directly with a public key. Row-Level Security policies are the only thing stopping one user from reading everyone's data.

walk.title: Protecting a Supabase table
steps: Table notes with owner_id. The frontend queries it with the public anon key.
RLS disabled: anyone can open DevTools, copy the key and run select * from notes. Every user's notes leak.
Enable RLS: now every query returns nothing until you add policies.
Add policy: users can select notes where owner_id = auth.uid(). Add similar insert/update policies.
Test with two accounts: each sees only their own notes, even with a raw query.

terms: Attribute-based access control: rules on properties of user and resource.
Row-level security: per-row access rules enforced by the database.
One system serving many separate customers (tenants).
insights: In multi-tenant apps, a missing tenant filter on one query is a catastrophic leak. RLS or a mandatory query layer prevents it.
Roles alone get messy (“editor-but-only-for-region-X”). Add attribute rules when roles multiply.
Test authorization like features: write tests that prove users cannot see others' data.

prod.summary: In production, authorization models fail at the edges: a new table without RLS, a background job running as a bypass role, a role nobody can explain, or a policy that turns a 5 ms query into a 2 s one. Seniors check that tenant isolation is enforced in one place, that bypass credentials are rare and server-only, and that permission rules have tests just like features.
checklist: Every table in an exposed schema has RLS enabled with explicit policies for select, insert, update and delete; a CI check fails on tables without RLS.
Policies use indexed columns (org_id, owner_id) and Supabase policies wrap functions as (select auth.uid()) so they run once per query, not per row.
Bypass credentials (service_role/secret keys, owner roles) are used only by server code and are absent from client bundles (grep the build output).
UPDATE policies state WITH CHECK explicitly. If it is omitted, Postgres reuses USING for the new row; a copied WITH CHECK (true) lets users move rows to another tenant.
Remember that permissive policies are OR-ed: one broad policy (USING (true) “for admins”) opens the table for everyone it applies to.
Permissions are defined as data or policy files, with tests for “user A cannot see tenant B”.
Role list is reviewed; roles that differ in one permission are merged into attributes or policies.
Admin and support access to tenant data is logged and, ideally, requires a reason.
numbers: Postgres: with RLS enabled and no policies, the default is deny-all for normal roles; table owners bypass RLS unless ALTER TABLE … FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY is set.
Supabase is deprecating the legacy anon and service_role keys in favour of sb_publishable_… and sb_secret_… keys by the end of 2026.
Supabase's docs report that wrapping auth.uid() as (select auth.uid()) in policies can speed up queries by orders of magnitude on large tables.
failures: Security researcher: “I can read every row of your profiles table with your public key.”
A table was created by SQL migration with RLS off. Enable RLS, add policies, and add a CI query that lists tables in exposed schemas where relrowsecurity is false.
The orders page takes 3 s after enabling RLS; EXPLAIN shows a sequential scan with a function call per row.
The policy calls a function per row and the filter column has no index. Index org_id, wrap auth.uid() in a subselect, and add the same filter in the app query to help the planner.
A user moved their own document into another company's workspace.
The UPDATE policy had WITH CHECK (true), copied from a template, so only the old row was checked, not the new org_id. Use WITH CHECK (org_id = current_org()) and test moving a row across tenants.
A support script leaked data across tenants.
It ran with the service role, which bypasses RLS, and forgot a tenant filter. Run scripts as a normal role with the tenant set (SET app.org_id), or require a tenant argument and test it.

code.title: Tenant isolation with Postgres RLS
code.src:
ALTER TABLE documents ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
ALTER TABLE documents FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY; -- owner is not exempt either

CREATE INDEX ON documents (org_id);

-- The app sets the tenant per transaction: SET LOCAL app.org_id = '…'
CREATE POLICY tenant_read ON documents
  FOR SELECT
  USING (org_id = current_setting('app.org_id')::uuid);

CREATE POLICY tenant_write ON documents
  FOR UPDATE
  USING      (org_id = current_setting('app.org_id')::uuid)  -- which rows you may touch
  WITH CHECK (org_id = current_setting('app.org_id')::uuid); -- what they may become

CREATE POLICY tenant_insert ON documents
  FOR INSERT
  WITH CHECK (org_id = current_setting('app.org_id')::uuid);

-- Only editors may delete
CREATE POLICY editor_delete ON documents
  FOR DELETE
  USING (org_id = current_setting('app.org_id')::uuid
         AND current_setting('app.role') IN ('owner', 'editor'));
code.note: With a connection pool, use SET LOCAL inside a transaction; a plain SET stays on the pooled connection and the next request may run with the previous tenant.

qs.s: Your app uses RLS with SET app.org_id = … at the start of each request and a shared connection pool. Occasionally users see another tenant's data. Likely cause?
o: RLS is not reliable
The tenant setting persists on the pooled connection; when a request skips or fails before setting it, the previous tenant's value is used. Use SET LOCAL inside a transaction
Postgres caches query results across users
The index on org_id is missing
qs.e: Session-level settings outlive the request on pooled connections. SET LOCAL resets at transaction end, and a missing setting then fails closed (error) instead of using stale state.

qs.s: documents has RLS enabled with a correct tenant policy, but not FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY. A nightly export job connects as the role that owns the table and has a bug: it forgets its WHERE org_id = …. What does the job see?
o: Only the first tenant's rows
Nothing, because RLS denies by default
An error, because no tenant is set
Every tenant's rows: the table owner bypasses RLS unless FORCE is set
qs.e: RLS does not apply to the table owner, superusers or BYPASSRLS roles by default. Run jobs as a normal role, or set FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY so even the owner is filtered.

qs.s: A SaaS has roles admin, editor, viewer, plus “editor-for-EU-only”, “viewer-but-can-export”, and 30 more variations. What is the usual next step?
o: Keep adding roles; RBAC scales
Give everyone admin and log actions
Move all checks into the frontend
Keep a few base roles and express the special cases as attributes and policies (ABAC) or relationships (ReBAC)
qs.e: Role explosion is the signal that rules depend on attributes (region, resource owner) or relationships (shared with). Policy engines like Cerbos, OPA or OpenFGA handle that without a role per combination.

qs.s: Read these Supabase policies. What does a normal signed-in user see?

code.title: policies.sql

o: Only their own documents, because the stricter policy wins
Nothing, because two policies conflict
Only documents for admins

Every document: permissive policies are combined with OR, and the second one applies to every authenticated user. Check admin status inside the policy (e.g. USING ((SELECT is_admin()))) or use a separate database role
qs.e: The comment says “admins”, but nothing in the policy checks it. Postgres combines permissive policies with OR, so the broadest one wins. Restrictive policies (AS RESTRICTIVE) are combined with AND and are the tool for mandatory conditions like tenant checks.

qs.s: RLS is enabled on documents with correct policies. A developer adds this view for the frontend. What happens when users query it through the Supabase API?

code.title: migration.sql
code.src:
CREATE VIEW public.team_documents AS
  SELECT d.id, d.title, d.owner_id, t.name AS team
  FROM documents d
  JOIN teams t ON t.id = d.team_id;

o: The view runs with its owner's privileges by default, so RLS on documents is bypassed and users see every row. Create it WITH (security_invoker = true) (PostgreSQL 15+) or do not expose it
RLS applies automatically to views, so users see only their rows
The query fails, because views cannot read RLS tables
Only the teams table's RLS applies
qs.e: A normal view checks permissions as the view owner (often postgres, which bypasses RLS). security_invoker makes the view check permissions and policies as the calling user. Supabase's security advisor flags these views.

qs.s: You are building document sharing like Google Drive: folders inside folders, sharing with users and groups, and permissions inherited from parent folders. Which model fits best?
o: RBAC with one role per folder
Relationship-based access control (ReBAC), e.g. OpenFGA or SpiceDB, where permissions are derived from relationships like “member of group”, “parent folder”, “viewer of”
ABAC with a rule per document
Postgres RLS with one policy per user
qs.e: Inheritance through folders and groups is a graph problem. ReBAC systems (based on Google's Zanzibar) store relationships and answer “can user X view doc Y?” by walking them. Roles per folder explode in number, and per-user policies do not scale.

qs.s: After enabling RLS, the orders list takes 1.8 s. Read the plan. What is the fix?

code.title: EXPLAIN ANALYZE
code.src:
Seq Scan on orders  (cost=0.00..48210.00 rows=10 width=64)
                    (actual time=0.031..1840.212 rows=37 loops=1)
  Filter: (org_id = (current_setting('app.org_id'::text))::uuid)
  Rows Removed by Filter: 1999963
Planning Time: 0.140 ms
Execution Time: 1840.301 ms

o: Disable RLS; it is slow by design
Increase work_mem
Add an index on orders(org_id) (or a composite one matching the page's sort, like (org_id, created_at DESC))
Cache the result for every user
qs.e: The policy adds a filter on org_id, but there is no index, so Postgres reads 2 million rows to keep 37. RLS filters are just WHERE conditions; they need the same indexes. work_mem affects sorts and hashes, not this scan.

interview.q: When do you choose RBAC, ABAC or ReBAC? Give examples.
answer: RBAC: a few stable roles with clear permissions (admin, editor, viewer in an internal tool). Easy to explain and audit.
ABAC: rules depend on attributes of user, resource or context (same region, owner, business hours, data classification). Use a policy engine (OPA, Cerbos) when rules multiply.
ReBAC: permissions follow relationships and inheritance (sharing, folders, teams, orgs). Use OpenFGA or SpiceDB when the graph is deep.
Most products mix them: roles inside a tenant, attributes for special cases, relationships for sharing.
Whatever the model: one decision point, deny by default, tests for “cannot” cases, and audit logs.
followups: How do you keep a policy engine's data in sync with your database?
How do you list “all documents a user can see” efficiently?

interview.q: We are on Supabase. How do you make sure no table leaks data?
answer: RLS enabled on every table in exposed schemas, with explicit policies per operation; a CI query fails if any table has relrowsecurity = false.
Views created with security_invoker = true; SECURITY DEFINER functions kept out of exposed schemas or with explicit checks and a fixed search_path.
Secret / service-role key only on the server; grep the client build for it.
Policies use (SELECT auth.uid()) and indexed columns; UPDATE policies have explicit WITH CHECK.
Tests with two real users against the REST API, plus Supabase's security advisor in CI.
followups: How do you handle admin tooling?
What changes with the new publishable and secret keys?

interview.q: Should authorization live in the application or in the database with RLS? What are the trade-offs?
answer: RLS: enforced for every query path (ORM, raw SQL, BI tools, the Supabase API), so a forgotten filter fails closed.
RLS costs: harder to debug and test, needs per-transaction context (SET LOCAL) with pooled connections, bypass roles must be controlled, and policies affect query plans.
App layer: richer logic (external calls, complex rules), easier unit tests, but every code path must remember to call it.
Common answer: tenant isolation in RLS (simple, mandatory), fine-grained business rules in the application or a policy engine.
Either way, test the “cannot” cases end to end.
followups: How do you use RLS with PgBouncer in transaction mode?
How would you migrate an existing app to RLS safely?

diagrams.caption: What to notice: the two ways to leak everything are a table without RLS and a bypass role. That is why the secret/service_role key must stay on the server.

codeCheck.detail: Run as a non-superuser role (superusers bypass RLS): each tenant saw only its own rows, WITH CHECK blocked a cross-tenant insert, and a viewer could not DELETE while an editor could.

one: Risks that come through your dependencies, build tools and CI rather than your own code.
an: Your restaurant's food is only as safe as your suppliers. One contaminated ingredient poisons every dish.
how: Threats: typosquatted packages (reqeusts), hijacked maintainer accounts publishing malicious versions (often via phishing), malicious install scripts, self-spreading worms that steal npm tokens and republish, compromised CI actions, dependency confusion between internal and public names.

Defences: lockfiles with npm ci, review dependency additions, a minimum release age before installing new versions (pnpm minimumReleaseAge, npm min-release-age, Dependabot cooldown), disable install scripts by default (pnpm 10 does this), pin GitHub Actions to commit SHAs, vulnerability scanning (npm audit, Dependabot, Snyk, Socket), provenance and trusted publishing (SLSA, Sigstore, npm OIDC), restrict CI secrets.
An SBOM (software bill of materials) lists what is inside your build, so you can answer “are we affected?” quickly.
why: A typical frontend pulls in 1,000+ transitive packages. Real incidents hit thousands of companies at once: event-stream (2018), ua-parser-js (2021), xz-utils (2024), the tj-actions/changed-files GitHub Action (March 2025), the phished maintainer account behind chalk and debug (September 2025, about 2.6 billion weekly downloads), and the Shai-Hulud npm worms (September and November 2025). “Software Supply Chain Failures” is A03 in the OWASP Top 10:2025.
trade: Zero dependencies is unrealistic. Be deliberate: prefer well-maintained packages, avoid adding a library for ten lines of code.

myth.m: npm audit is clean, so we are safe.
myth.r: It only knows about reported vulnerabilities. Freshly published malicious versions are not in the database yet.

q.s: Cheapest strong step against a compromised third-party GitHub Action?
o: Use @main
Pin actions to a full commit SHA and limit the token permissions of the workflow
Disable CI
Use more actions
q.e: Tags can be moved to malicious code; SHAs cannot. Least-privilege tokens limit damage.

lab: Run npm audit and npx better-npm-audit (or Socket) on a project; read what each finding means.
Pin every GitHub Action in one repo to a commit SHA and set permissions: contents: read at the top of the workflow.
Generate an SBOM with syft or npm sbom.
docs: SLSA: Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts
GitHub: Security hardening for GitHub Actions

plain:
Your app includes hundreds of npm packages written by strangers, plus build tools and CI actions. If any of them is malicious or hijacked, your app is too. That is a supply-chain attack.

You cannot avoid dependencies, but you can choose them carefully, pin them, and limit what a compromised one can reach.
bridge: npm install can run install scripts from any package in your dependency tree, on your laptop and in CI, with access to your environment variables.

walk.title: How a hijacked package spreads
steps: An attacker steals a popular package maintainer's npm password.
They publish version 3.4.1 with a hidden script that sends environment variables to their server.
Thousands of projects using ^3.4.0 install it on the next npm install, including CI runners with deploy keys.
Projects using lockfiles and npm ci stay on 3.4.0 until someone updates deliberately.
The malicious version is removed within hours, but every CI secret it saw must be rotated.

terms: Everything that goes into your software that you did not write.
Malicious packages with names like popular ones (e.g. reqeusts).
Software bill of materials: a list of every component in your build.
insights: Before adding a package, check: maintained? popular? necessary? Ten lines of your own code beat a tiny dependency.
Your CI runner is the prize: install scripts there can read deploy keys. Keep secrets out of install and test jobs that do not need them.
Response speed matters as much as prevention: with lockfiles and an SBOM, “were we affected?” takes minutes, not days.

prod.summary: In production, supply-chain security is about the path from npm install to a deployed artifact: what can run during install, what CI secrets those scripts can see, how fast a bad version reaches you, and whether you can prove what you shipped. After the 2025 npm worms, seniors add a release-age delay, block install scripts by default, move publishing to OIDC trusted publishing, and pin CI actions by SHA.
checklist: CI installs with npm ci / pnpm install --frozen-lockfile; lockfile changes are reviewed like code.
New versions must be a few days old before install (minimumReleaseAge / min-release-age / Dependabot cooldown), with exceptions for urgent security fixes.
Dependency install scripts are off by default and allowed per package (pnpm onlyBuiltDependencies, or --ignore-scripts).
Third-party GitHub Actions are pinned to full commit SHAs, and workflows set minimal permissions.
Packages you publish use trusted publishing (OIDC) from CI, with provenance, and maintainers use 2FA with phishing-resistant keys.
Internal package names are under a scope you own (@company/…) and the registry config maps that scope to your private registry (stops dependency confusion).
An SBOM is generated per release so “are we affected by package X version Y?” is a query, not a week of work.
numbers: npm (December 2025): classic tokens were revoked; new write-enabled granular tokens default to 7-day expiry with a 90-day maximum.
pnpm 10 (January 2025) stopped running dependency lifecycle scripts by default; pnpm 10.16 added minimumReleaseAge (in minutes); npm 11.10 (February 2026) added min-release-age (in days).
The September 2025 chalk/debug compromise affected 18 packages with about 2.6 billion weekly downloads; Shai-Hulud 2.0 (November 2025) backdoored about 800 npm packages.
The tj-actions/changed-files compromise (CVE-2025-30066) moved existing version tags to a malicious commit, so every workflow using @v35-style tags ran it; SHA-pinned workflows did not.
failures: Security advisory: a package in your tree was malicious for 3 hours yesterday. Did you install it?

Check lockfile history and CI logs for that version. If any CI job or laptop installed it, rotate every secret that environment could see (npm, cloud, GitHub tokens). A release-age delay would have kept you out of that 3-hour window.
CI logs show an unknown script running curl … | sh during npm install.
A dependency's postinstall. Stop the pipeline, rotate secrets, and switch to scripts-off-by-default with an explicit allowlist.
Your internal package billing-utils resolves to a public npm package with a higher version number.
Dependency confusion. Rename to a scoped name you control (@acme/billing-utils), map the scope to your private registry, and reserve the scope on the public registry.
A popular Action's tag v4 suddenly runs different code that prints secrets to logs.
Tags are mutable. Pin to a commit SHA (with the tag as a comment), let Dependabot update the SHA, and remove broad secrets from jobs that do not need them.

code.title: Hardened CI: SHA-pinned actions, least privilege, scripts off
code.src:
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: ci
on: [pull_request]

permissions:
  contents: read            # nothing can push with this token

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      # Vulnerable: uses: actions/checkout@v7   (tags can be moved)
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: actions/setup-node@820762786026740c76f36085b0efc47a31fe5020 # v7.0.0
        with:
          node-version: 22
      - run: npm ci --ignore-scripts   # no install scripts from dependencies
      - run: npm rebuild esbuild       # allow the one native package that needs it
      - run: npm test

# .npmrc (npm 11.10+): only install versions published at least 3 days ago
# min-release-age=3
code.note: Pinning by SHA makes the code you run immutable. Look up the SHA for the tag you trust and keep the tag as a comment so updates stay readable.

qs.s: A worm publishes malicious versions of popular packages and they are removed after 6 hours. Your project uses lockfiles and Dependabot opens update PRs daily. Which setting would most likely have kept you safe?
o: Running npm audit in CI
A minimum release age / cooldown (e.g. 3 days) for new versions
Using ^ ranges instead of exact versions
Hosting your own CDN
qs.e: Most malicious versions are found and removed within hours to days. Waiting a few days before adopting new versions avoids that window. npm audit only knows about issues already reported.

qs.s: Your company publishes an npm package from CI using a long-lived npm token stored as a GitHub secret. What is the recommended replacement in 2026?
o: A classic token with 2FA disabled
Rotate the same token yearly
Trusted publishing (OIDC) from the CI workflow, so there is no stored publish token, with provenance enabled
Publish manually from a developer laptop
qs.e: Stolen long-lived tokens are how worms spread. With trusted publishing, the registry trusts a specific workflow identity and issues short-lived credentials per run. Classic tokens no longer exist on npm.

qs.s: SBOMs are generated for every release. A critical CVE is announced in libfoo 2.3.1. What does the SBOM let you do that a lockfile in each repo does not?
o: Fix the CVE automatically
Block the package from npm
Query all shipped artifacts across services at once to see which deployed versions contain libfoo 2.3.1, including container base image packages
Nothing; they contain the same data
qs.e: An SBOM describes what was actually built and shipped (including OS packages in images), and can be stored centrally. Lockfiles live in many repos, can differ from what is deployed, and miss non-npm components.

qs.s: This workflow runs tests for pull requests from forks. What is wrong?

code.title: .github/workflows/pr-test.yml
code.src:
on: pull_request_target
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
        with:
          ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}
      - run: npm ci && npm test
        env:
          NPM_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.NPM_TOKEN }}

o: Nothing; the action is pinned to a SHA
Only that npm ci should use --ignore-scripts

pull_request_target runs with the base repo's secrets and a write-capable token, and this job checks out and runs the fork's code. Any PR author can steal NPM_TOKEN. Use pull_request for untrusted code
Forks cannot trigger pull_request_target
qs.e: This is the “pwn request” pattern. pull_request_target exists for trusted tasks like labelling; it must never build or run PR code. Pinning the action protects against a compromised action, not against the PR's own package.json scripts and tests.

qs.s: Your .npmrc has @acme:registry=https://npm.acme.internal/. Which dependency is exposed to dependency confusion?

code.title: package.json (excerpt)

o: @acme/ui, because it uses a caret range
acme-billing-utils: it is unscoped, so npm resolves it from the public registry, where anyone can publish that name
react, because it comes from the public registry
None; an exact version prevents it
qs.e: Only the @acme scope is mapped to the private registry. An unscoped internal name falls through to npmjs.com. Move it under the scope, and claim the scope on the public registry. An exact version does not help if an attacker publishes that exact version publicly first.

qs.s: npm view some-lib shows a provenance attestation linking the release to a GitHub repo, commit and workflow. What does it prove?
o: That this tarball was built by that workflow from that commit in that repository, and not uploaded from someone's laptop; it does not prove the code is safe
That the code has been security-audited
That the maintainer used 2FA
That no dependency of the package is malicious
qs.e: Provenance answers “where did this come from?”. That stops a stolen npm token from publishing a version that looks like it came from CI. A malicious commit in the repo, or a compromised workflow, still produces valid provenance.

qs.s: Your Dockerfile starts with FROM node:22. Builds on different days give different results, and one day a scanner finds a new critical CVE. What is the recommended practice?

code.title: Dockerfile
code.src:
FROM node:22
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
COPY . .
CMD ["node", "server.js"]

o: Use node:latest so you always have the newest fixes
Never update the base image once it works
Copy the Node binary from your laptop
Pin the base image by digest (FROM node:22-slim@sha256:…) so builds are reproducible, and let Renovate or Dependabot open PRs when the digest changes, so updates are deliberate and tested
qs.e: Tags are mutable, like Git tags on Actions. A digest is the exact image. Pinning without automated updates would leave you on old, vulnerable images, so pair it with a bot. A smaller base (-slim or distroless) also means fewer packages to patch.

interview.q: A popular npm package in our tree was compromised yesterday for a few hours. Walk me through your response.
answer: Scope: which repos have it in their lockfile, and did any install in the window pull the bad version? Check lockfile history, CI logs, registry proxy logs, and developer machines.
If installed anywhere: treat that environment as compromised. Rotate every secret it could read (npm, GitHub, cloud, deploy keys), and review the audit logs for use of those secrets.
Check whether a bad build was deployed; rebuild from clean lockfiles and redeploy if so.
Communicate: affected teams, and customers if shipped artifacts were affected.
Prevent: minimum release age, scripts off by default, an internal registry proxy, OIDC publishing, and secrets kept out of install steps.
followups: How would an SBOM have changed this response?
What would you check on developer laptops?

interview.q: How would you harden our CI/CD pipeline against supply-chain attacks?
answer: Inputs: lockfiles with npm ci, a release-age delay, install scripts off by default, base images pinned by digest.
Actions: third-party actions pinned to SHAs, updated by a bot; avoid pull_request_target with PR code.
Secrets: minimal workflow permissions, OIDC to cloud and npm instead of long-lived tokens, secrets scoped to the jobs and environments that need them.
Outputs: build once, sign or attest (provenance, SLSA), deploy the same artifact; generate an SBOM per release.
Protect the pipeline config: branch protection, required reviews for workflow changes, CODEOWNERS on .github/.
followups: Which of these would you do first, with one week?
How do you handle self-hosted runners?

interview.q: How do you decide whether to add a new dependency?
answer: Need: could we write it in under ~50 lines, or use the platform (Node has fetch, crypto.randomUUID, util.parseArgs)?
Health: maintainers, release history, open issues, download trend, provenance or trusted publishing.
Cost: size of the transitive tree, install scripts, native builds, licence.
Risk: what it can reach at runtime (network, file system, secrets) and in CI.
Process: a short review for new direct dependencies, and a tool like Socket or npm audit signatures in CI.
followups: How would you remove a deeply used dependency?
Would you vendor a small package?

diagrams.title: A hijacked package meets three defences
diagrams.src:
flowchart TD
  A["Maintainer's npm password stolen"] --> B["3.4.1 published with an install script"]
  B --> C{"How does your CI install?"}
  C -- "npm install with ^3.4.0" --> D["Gets 3.4.1"]
  D --> E{"Install scripts allowed?"}
  E -- "yes" --> F["Script sends env vars and CI secrets out"]
  F --> R["Rotate every secret it saw"]
  E -- "no, scripts off by default" --> G["Script never runs"]
  C -- "npm ci with lockfile" --> H["Stays on 3.4.0"]
  C -- "release-age delay of 3 days" --> I["3.4.1 too new, skipped until removed"]
diagrams.caption: What to notice: the malicious version is usually removed within hours. A lockfile or a release-age delay keeps you out of that window; scripts-off stops the payload even if the version arrives.
